revised.title: Buffer target and the payday it is reached
revised.answers: On which payday will a buffer for my must-pay costs be ready?
revised.short: When will my buffer be ready?
revised.intro: Answers one question: on which payday is a buffer for your must-pay costs fully set aside?

inputs.label: Must-pay costs a month
inputs.hint: Rent or room share, food, getting to work or college, your phone, and course costs you must pay: what still arrives in a month with no pay. Leave out spending that would stop.
inputs.source: example: each lesson's own total. in/money-basics/one-month-buffer document: room share ₹2,500 + food ₹1,800 + travel ₹600 + phone and data ₹300 + course materials ₹300 = ₹5,500. eu/money-basics/three-month-buffer document: rent share €400 + transport €60 + phone €20 + food €250 = €730. us/money-basics/first-cushion details: rent share $600 + phone $45 + getting to work $120 + food $290 = $1,055.
inputs.validation: Required. Read with readAmount (see maths). Blank, unreadable, 0 or negative: 'Enter your must-pay costs for one month, above 0.' Above 1,000,000,000, or too long to be a finite number: 'This works with amounts up to {1e9 via number(1e9, locale)}' (en-IN prints 1,00,00,00,000). NumberField gets min="0" max="1000000000". Any error hides the Figure, ledger, facts and sentence.

inputs.label: Months to cover
inputs.hint: Per edition, from regions.ts buffer.monthsHint. India: 'The lesson starts at one month of costs.' Europe: 'The lesson uses three: the length the EU's 2023 survey asked about, reported in the Commission's 2025 strategy. A measure, not a rule.' United States: 'The US lesson starts with $400, then one month of must-pay costs.'
inputs.source: example: each lesson's own number. Only Europe cites a source: European Commission, Communication on a Financial Literacy Strategy for the EU, COM(2025) 681 (30 September 2025), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0681, reporting Flash Eurobarometer 525 (2023), https://europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/2953: almost half (49%) of people aged 18 to 65 lack emergency savings to cover living expenses for at least three months without borrowing. It reports a survey measure and sets no target (checked 22 September 2026 through the document's indexed text; EUR-Lex returned an empty page to the fetcher, as the skeptic found).
inputs.validation: Required, between 1 and 24, fractions allowed (1.5 is fine; 0.5 is not). Blank, 0, 0.5, negative, above 24 or unreadable: 'Enter between 1 and 24 months.' NumberField gets min="1" max="24".

inputs.label: Already set aside for this
inputs.hint: Only money kept apart for a bill you did not choose, not this month's spending money.
inputs.source: example
inputs.validation: Blank counts as 0 and is not an error. Negative: 'Enter 0 or more.' Above 1,000,000,000 or not finite: 'This works with amounts up to {1e9 in the locale}.' max="1000000000".

inputs.label: Moved aside each {paydayWord} (India and Europe 'payday', United States 'paycheck')
inputs.hint: The amount moved aside the day pay lands, the same every time.
inputs.source: example: the three buffer lessons (India ₹2,000 a month, 'Pay minus costs'; Europe €185 each payday, the goal screen; US $50 a paycheck, every two weeks)
inputs.validation: Blank or 0 is not an error: it gives the 'no amount' state (no date, the sentence asks for an amount). Negative: 'Enter 0 or more.' Above 1,000,000,000 or not finite: 'This works with amounts up to {1e9 in the locale}.' Amounts are counted in whole cents, so anything under half a cent counts as 0. max="1000000000".

inputs.label: How often you are paid
inputs.hint: Turns a count of paydays into weeks or months.
inputs.source: example: India and Europe lessons move money monthly; the US lesson is paid every two weeks
inputs.validation: Allow-list, never an error message: the value is used only if isPayFrequency(value) is true; any other value from a # or ? link, the DOM or a default falls back to the edition default before it reaches bufferPlan, and that fallback also sets the select's value and what Copy link writes.

rules.label: $400, the hypothetical emergency expense in the Federal Reserve's 2025 household survey (fielded October 2025, published 13 May 2026): its example, not a rule
rules.sourceTitle: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, press release: Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (13 May 2026). 'The share who would cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent also remained unchanged from 2024 at 63 percent'; the survey was fielded in October 2025. The report's savings chapter (https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-savings-investments.htm) defines cash or its equivalent as cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement.

outputs: Headline Figure, dated state: value '{PaydayWord} {n}' (India 'Payday 3', Europe 'Payday 12', US 'Paycheck 22'); label 'about {count} {month|months|week|weeks}, counting your next {paydayWord} as {paydayWord} 1' (India 'about 3 months…', Europe 'about 12 months…', US 'about 10 months, counting your next paycheck as paycheck 1'). When n = 1 the label is 'your next {paydayWord}'.
Headline Figure, covered state: value 'Covered now', label 'Already set aside is at or above the target'. No payday count and no months line.
Headline Figure, no-amount state: value '—', label 'Add what you move each {paydayWord} to see the date'.
Headline Figure, too-long state (more than 120 months away): value 'More than 10 years', label 'at {perPayday} each {paydayWord}'. No payday number.

Ledger, dated state: 'Buffer target: {essentials} × {months} {month|months}' → target (₹5,500 / €2,190 / $1,055); 'Already set aside' (minus) → saved; 'Still to set aside' (subtotal, single rule) → toGo; 'Moved each {paydayWord}' → perPayday; '{PaydayWord}s needed: {quotient}, rounded up' (main, double rule) → n (India '2.75, rounded up' → 3; Europe '11.84, rounded up' → 12; US '21.1, rounded up' → 22). When the division is exact the label is '{PaydayWord}s needed' with no 'rounded up'; when the quotient is not whole but shows as whole at 2 decimals it reads 'just over {floor}'.
Ledger, covered, no-amount and too-long states: the first two rows, then 'Still to set aside' as the main (double-ruled) row (covered: ₹0).

Fact, dated state: label 'Held on {paydayWord} {n}, {over} above the target' (or ', exactly the target' when over is 0), value heldAtEnd (India ₹6,000 with ₹500; Europe €2,220 with €30; US $1,100 with $45).

Fact, US only: label '$400, the Federal Reserve survey's example emergency expense, not a rule: about {count} months' and value 'Paycheck {m}' (defaults: 'about 4 months', 'Paycheck 8'). Shown only when the page passed a milestone (US edition), the displayed currency is USD, there are no field errors, perPayday > 0, saved < $400 < target, and the milestone falls within 10 years. It can show in the too-long state; otherwise nothing takes its place.

Assumption notice, every non-error state: 'The same amount every payday, counting your next payday as payday 1, and no interest: only what you move sets the date. To add an example rate, use Savings growth.' ('Savings growth' links to /<edition>/tools/savings; US text says paycheck.)
Error state: only the error texts under the fields and the line 'Fix the field marked above to see the date.' No Figure, ledger, facts or sentence.
US page only, static and outside the island: a RulesLine with lead 'Figure checked 22 September 2026:' then the milestone rule's label and source link.
revised.resultSentence: Placeholders: {M} is months formatted with 0–2 decimals; {mo} is 'month' when M = 1, else 'months'; {count} {unit} comes from timeAway, singular when count = 1; money is exact() in the displayed locale. DATED, saved = 0: '{M} {mo} of these costs is {target}. Moving {perPayday} each {paydayWord}, you reach it on {paydayWord} {n}, about {count} {unit} away, holding {held}, {over} above it.' DATED, saved > 0: '{M} {mo} of these costs is {target}. With {saved} already set aside and {perPayday} moved each {paydayWord}, you reach it on {paydayWord} {n}, about {count} {unit} away, holding {held}, {over} above it.' When n = 1, replace 'on {paydayWord} {n}, about {count} {unit} away' with 'on your next {paydayWord}'. When over = 0, the ending is 'holding exactly {target}.' COVERED: '{saved} already covers the {target} target, {surplus} above it.' (surplus 0: '{saved} already covers the {target} target.') NO AMOUNT (perPayday blank or 0, toGo > 0): '{M} {mo} of these costs is {target}, and {toGo} is still to set aside. Add what you move each {paydayWord} to see the date.' TOO LONG: '{M} {mo} of these costs is {target}. At {perPayday} each {paydayWord}, the {toGo} still to set aside takes more than 10 years; a larger amount brings the date closer.' ERROR (any field problem): 'Fix the field marked above to see the date.' Opening sentences: India '1 month of these costs is ₹5,500. Moving ₹2,000 each payday, you reach it on payday 3, about 3 months away, holding ₹6,000, ₹500 above it.' Europe '3 months of these costs is €2,190. Moving €185 each payday, you reach it on payday 12, about 12 months away, holding €2,220, €30 above it.' US '1 month of these costs is $1,055. Moving $50 each paycheck, you reach it on paycheck 22, about 10 months away, holding $1,100, $45 above it.' The sentence says 'is', never 'should', and never 'to spare'.
revised.maths:
All pure, in src/lib/finance.ts unless noted; no interest and no rate input anywhere.
(1) toCents(x: number): number = Math.round(Number((x * 100).toPrecision(15))). toPrecision strips binary error before rounding: 1.005 → 101 cents, where Math.round(1.005 * 100) gives 100. roundMoney(x) = toCents(x) / 100. Both exported and shared with the batch (this is the registry's round2).
(2) PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR: Record<PayFrequency, number> = { weekly: 52, fortnightly: 26, 'twice-monthly': 24, monthly: 12 }. isPayFrequency(v: string): v is PayFrequency uses Object.hasOwn(PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR, v), so 'toString', 'every two weeks' and 'abc' are false. BUFFER_LIMITS = { maxAmount: 1e9, minMonths: 1, maxMonths: 24, maxMonthsAway: 120 }.
(3) readAmount(raw: string): { value: number | null; tooBig: boolean } (tool-kit.tsx, shared). Trim the text; blank gives { null, false }. If it matches /^[+-]?(\d+\.?\d*|\.\d+)(e[+-]?\d+)?$/i, use it as it is. Otherwise strip everything except digits, '.' and '-' ('1,00,000' and '₹500' pass) and test the pattern again. No match gives { null, false }. A Number() that is not finite gives { null, true }. −0 becomes 0. So '1e5' → 100000, where the kit's toNumber strips the e and gives 15, and a 400-digit entry is too-big, where toNumber turns it into 0.
(4) bufferInputProblems(raw: { essentials; months; saved; perPayday }): Partial<Record<key, 'required' | 'too-big' | 'months-range' | 'negative'>>. essentials: value null or ≤ 0 → required; tooBig or > 1e9 → too-big. months: null, tooBig, < 1 or > 24 → months-range, and fractions are allowed. saved and perPayday: null counts as 0 with no problem; < 0 → negative; tooBig or > 1e9 → too-big. The island maps the codes to the messages in inputs.validation.
(5) timeAway(paydays: number, paydaysPerYear: number): { unit: 'week' | 'month'; count: number }. With m = paydays × 12 / paydaysPerYear: if m < 1, return { week, max(1, Math.round(paydays × 52 / paydaysPerYear)) }; otherwise return { month, Math.round(m) }. Payday 1 is the next payday (or today if the reader was paid today), so the figure is 'about' and can be out by up to one pay period.
(6) bufferPlan(essentials: number, months: number, saved: number, perPayday: number, paydaysPerYear: number, milestone?: number): BufferPlan | null.
It returns null in these cases: any argument is not finite; paydaysPerYear is not 52, 26, 24 or 12; essentials ≤ 0 or > 1e9; months < 1 or > 24; saved or perPayday < 0 or > 1e9. Because of this, a field error can never reach a result, which settles precedence.
Otherwise it works in integer cents: e = toCents(essentials), s = toCents(saved), p = toCents(perPayday); target t = Math.round(e × months); toGo = max(0, t − s); surplus = max(0, s − t).
Milestone, worked out in every state: with M = toCents(milestone), if milestone is given, p > 0 and s < M < t, then mp = ceil((M − s) / p). It is kept only if mp × 12 / ppy ≤ 120, and then milestoneAway = timeAway(mp, ppy). Otherwise both are null.
States:
- toGo = 0 → 'covered': paydays 0; quotient, away, heldAtEnd and overTarget are null.
- else p = 0 → 'no-amount': all of those null.
- else n = ceil(toGo / p), exact because both are integers under 2^53 (at most 2.4e12 cents). quotient = Math.round(toGo / p × 100) / 100 and exactDivision = (toGo % p === 0). If n × 12 / ppy > 120 → 'too-long' with paydays, away, heldAtEnd and overTarget null. Otherwise 'dated': paydays = n, away = timeAway(n, ppy), heldAtEnd = (s + n × p) / 100, overTarget = (s + n × p − t) / 100.
Every money output is cents ÷ 100. The type is BufferPlan = { state: 'covered' | 'no-amount' | 'too-long' | 'dated'; target: number; toGo: number; surplus: number; paydays: number | null; quotient: number | null; exactDivision: boolean; away: TimeAway | null; heldAtEnd: number | null; overTarget: number | null; milestonePayday: number | null; milestoneAway: TimeAway | null }.
(7) Island, src/islands/BufferTarget.tsx, id prefix 'bt', about 3 KB gz. freq = isPayFrequency(fields.paidEvery) ? fields.paidEvery : defaults.paidEvery, and that same value drives the select, the calculation and ToolActions' query. Then problems = bufferInputProblems(fields); if any exist, show only the errors. Otherwise plan = bufferPlan(values…, PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR[freq], showMilestone ? milestone.value : undefined), where showMilestone = milestone prop present && locale.currency === milestone.currency. The $400 is always printed with money(milestone.value, localeByCode('en-US')), never with the reader's locale. Money uses exact(), with decimals only when there are any. The quotient shows 0 to 2 decimals.

revised.howItWorks: Worked on the numbers on screen. With the Europe opening figures: 'The target is one month of your must-pay costs times the months you chose: €730 × 3 = €2,190. Anything already set aside comes off it. The rest is divided by what you move each payday and rounded up, because the target is passed on a payday, not between two: €2,190 ÷ €185 = 11.84, so payday 12, when you hold 12 × €185 = €2,220. Payday 1 is your next payday, or today if you were paid today, so the months shown can be out by up to one pay period. Weeks and months come from 52, 26, 24 or 12 paydays a year. Past 10 years no date is shown. What this leaves out: interest, since only what you move sets the date (Savings growth adds an example rate); a smaller or missed payday, which moves the date later, so try the smaller amount; and a bill paid from the buffer before it is full, after which the count starts again from what is left. It does not say how many months to hold, or where to keep the money.' Europe adds: 'Three months is the length the EU's 2023 survey asked about. Almost half of people aged 18 to 65 could not cover three months of living costs without borrowing (European Commission, Financial Literacy Strategy for the EU, 30 September 2025, linked). It is a measure, not a rule.' The United States adds: '$400 is the hypothetical emergency expense in the Federal Reserve's household survey, fielded in October 2025 and published on 13 May 2026. 63% of adults said they would cover it with cash or its equivalent, which the survey counts as cash, savings, or a credit card paid off at the next statement (report chapter linked). It is the survey's example, not a rule, and it is shown only while the currency is dollars.' No firm, bank or app is named.

foundationNeeds: src/lib/finance.ts: export toCents(x) = Math.round(Number((x * 100).toPrecision(15))) and roundMoney(x) = toCents(x) / 100 for the whole batch (the registry's round2). Why: Math.round(1.005 * 100) is 100, and a float division such as 150.15 ÷ 50.05 gives 3.0000000000000004, which rounds up to 4 paydays instead of 3.

src/lib/finance.ts: export PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR = { weekly: 52, fortnightly: 26, 'twice-monthly': 24, monthly: 12 }, `type PayFrequency = keyof typeof PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR` and isPayFrequency() (an own-key check). regions.ts re-exports the type rather than defining it, so finance.ts never imports regions.ts. Shared with take-home-pay's US paidEvery. Why: one allow-list for every pay-frequency value that can arrive from a link.

src/islands/tool-kit.tsx: SelectField({ id, label, value, options: { value; label }[], onChange, hint }), with the same `.field` markup as NumberField: a visible label, a hint span with id `${id}-hint`, and aria-describedby. It is built once, by whichever of take-home-pay or buffer-target lands first. Why: neither tool can ship without it, and the kit has none today.

src/islands/tool-kit.tsx Result: add `subtotal?: boolean`, which adds class `ledger-subtotal`. src/styles/base.css: `.ledger-subtotal { border-top: 1px solid var(--ink); margin-top: var(--space-2); }` and `.ledger-subtotal .ledger-label { color: var(--ink); font-weight: 700; }`, tokens only. Why: the ledger needs a single rule above 'Still to set aside' and a double rule only under the final payday count (BRAND_GUIDE §5). Today `main` is the only emphasis the kit has.

src/islands/tool-kit.tsx: export readAmount(raw) (see maths). New tools validate with it and never with toNumber. Why: toNumber('1e5') is 15, because it strips the e from a value a number input accepts, and a 400-digit entry becomes 0. Either would show a wrong date or the wrong error.

Edition rules and the currency picker: the $400 milestone is keyed on the page's edition. It lives only in the US entry of regions.ts (`buffer.milestone?: Rule & { currency: 'USD' }`, with Rule = { value, label, source, asOf } from the registry), and [tool].astro passes it as a prop only when that entry defines it. BufferTarget renders the milestone Fact only when the prop exists AND locale.currency === milestone.currency, and prints the amount with money(value, localeByCode('en-US')), never in the reader's locale. The CurrencyField stays on this tool, because the target, the transfers and the dates are the same in any currency and no computed figure reads the picker. Tools whose rules change a computed figure (take-home-pay, side-income-tax) should hide the CurrencyField instead; this tool does not need to.

changes: Lesson frontmatter (A1, B5; conflicts with the registry). Kept `tool: savings` on the India and Europe buffer lessons, whose growth explorables hand off to it, and added `moreTools: [buffer-target]`. Only the US lesson switches to `tool: buffer-target`. I rejected the registry's line making buffer-target the `tool` of in/one-month-buffer and eu/three-month-buffer, because the brief forbids changing `tool` where the explorable hands off to it. I used the registry's `moreTools` array instead of A's alsoTool string or B's alsoTools, so the batch has one field. Both skeptics' related-filter fix is applied under that name.

US $400 milestone and currency (A2, B1). The milestone is a Rule in the US entry only and is passed as a prop from the page. It shows only when the displayed currency is USD, and it is printed with a fixed en-US formatter, never the reader's locale. Stored as Rule & { currency: 'USD' } to fit the registry's Rule type. asOf is 2026-09-22, the date I re-checked the source, because the registry's Rule defines asOf as the date last checked; the registry had 2026-05-13, the publication date.

Europe €10 interest clause (A3, B12). Removed. The assumption line now reads the same in every edition, has no rate or interest figure, and links to Savings growth. I merged A's wording and B's wording, and added 'counting your next payday as payday 1' (A14, B4).

Essentials of 0 or blank (A4). Now a field error ('Enter your must-pay costs for one month, above 0.'). A asked for a unit test that bufferPlan(0, 1, 0, 100, 12) returns target 0. I changed it so bufferPlan returns null: a function that returns a target of 0 is what produced the '₹0 already covers ₹0' sentence. The test asserts null, and the e2e test asserts the error and no 'Covered now'.

Pay-frequency values (A5, B7, and the registry conflict). A wanted weekly/biweekly/semimonthly/monthly, B wanted '52'/'26'/'24'/'12', and the registry's PayFrequency is weekly/fortnightly/twice-monthly/monthly. I took the registry's slugs, which read clearly in a link and are shared with take-home-pay, with the allow-list parse and edition-default fallback both skeptics asked for. A's e2e test used '?paidEvery=fortnightly' as the invalid value, but that value is valid under the registry, so the fallback tests use B's 'abc', in both # and ? form. SelectField is built in tool-kit.tsx.

Covered state (A6). The Figure reads 'Covered now', with the label 'Already set aside is at or above the target'. The ledger closes on 'Still to set aside: ₹0'. The sentence says '{surplus} above it', not 'to spare', and the payday and months lines are hidden.

Milestone conditions (A7, B9). The Fact shows only when all of these hold: a milestone prop exists (US page), the currency is USD, there are no errors, perPayday > 0, saved < 400 < target, and the milestone falls within 10 years. Unit pins cover target 300, saved 400, perPayday 0, and the too-long and beyond-cap cases.

Essentials hint (A8, B14, which conflict). I kept A's fix and dropped B's 'Leave out what can shrink in a bad month', because it tells the reader to drop food, which the Europe lesson calls an essential. I added B's 'course costs you must pay', so the India default of ₹5,500 (which includes course materials) matches its own hint.

Months hint (A9, B2, B3). Now per edition, in regions.ts. Europe's wording is B's, checked against the source: the 2023 survey measured three months without borrowing, and the Commission's 2025 strategy reports it without setting a target. The hint adds 'a measure, not a rule' (A). The US hint follows the lesson's order: $400 first, then one month (B3). Only Europe cites EUR-Lex, plus Flash Eurobarometer 525 (B2). whyItHelps is not a shipped field, so B's rewording lives in the input's source note.

Cap (A10, B10). The cap is on time, not on the payday count: more than 120 months gives 'More than 10 years' and no payday number. Boundary pins at all four frequencies (520/521 weekly, 260/261, 240/241, 120/121).

Limits and rounding (A11, B11). Amounts are 0 to 1e9 with max= set, and months are 1 to 24 with fractions allowed, so 0.5 is an error. The error text is A's 'Enter between 1 and 24 months.', chosen over B's 'Between 1 and 24 months', to match the kit's verb-first messages. The size limit prints in the locale's own digits. bufferPlan guards finiteness, and the payday count uses integer cents rather than the 1e-9 epsilon, with a pin where float division is wrong (150.15 ÷ 50.05). I added readAmount, because the kit's toNumber reads '1e5' as 15 and a 400-digit entry as 0.

Error precedence (A12). Any field problem shows only the error texts and 'Fix the field marked above to see the date'. bufferPlan also returns null on the same inputs, so no result can leak. Unit and e2e tests cover saved ≥ target with perPayday −5.

Missing code (A13, B6). regions.ts gets the buffer defaults type, with monthsHint, monthsSource, paydayWord, milestone and scenario. SelectField and a Result `subtotal` variant are listed as kit work. The dependency on take-home-pay is dropped: whichever of the two lands first builds SelectField. The scenario strings are rewritten so they read correctly after 'It opens on an example:'.

Months precision and plurals (A14, B4, which conflict). I took B's whole months (and weeks when under a month) over A's '3.7 months', because it matches the lessons' 'about four months' and does not claim precision the payday-1 assumption cannot give. B asked for Math.ceil for weeks; I used Math.round with a minimum of 1, because ceil turns half a month (one twice-monthly payday) into 3 weeks instead of 2. I added a rule that n = 1 reads 'your next payday', so a buffer one payday away is never 'about 1 month' when it could be today. Plurals are handled: '1 month', '1.5 months', 'about 1 month'.

Ledger (B13). The ledger now runs: target ('{essentials} × {months}'), minus already set aside, 'Still to set aside' as a single-rule subtotal, 'Moved each payday', then '{Paydays} needed: 11.84, rounded up' as the double-ruled answer. The amount held and the amount above the target sit in a Fact below.

Milestone wording (A14, B8). The Fact says '$400, the Federal Reserve survey's example emergency expense, not a rule'. The 63% figure, 'cash or its equivalent' (defined in the report as cash, savings or a credit card paid off at the next statement), the October 2025 fieldwork and the 13 May 2026 publication date sit in How this is worked out and the RulesLine. I re-fetched both Federal Reserve pages on 22 September 2026. Months come out as 'about 4 months', not 3.7.

Firms in modelledOn (A15, B15). modelledOn and whyItHelps are internal and not part of this spec. No text naming NerdWallet, Chase, Practical Money Skills or any other firm reaches tools.ts, regions.ts, the island or How this is worked out. B could not verify the Chase 'rate 0% by default' and Practical Money Skills claims, so they are withdrawn rather than linked.

Other changes. Minutes are 2, not the registry's 1: there are five fields, and the ledger is worth reading. The intro now asks a single question. The hint for the amount moved each payday describes an assumption instead of giving an instruction.
risks: The payday-1 convention makes every duration approximate by up to one pay period. It is stated in the Figure label, the assumption line and How this is worked out, and n = 1 reads 'your next payday'.

Months is a reader's input that opens at each lesson's number, so a three-month default on the Europe page could still read as a target. The hint says 'a measure, not a rule', and the sentence uses 'is', never 'should'.
When a US reader has a non-dollar currency saved in lp:locale, the $400 Fact disappears silently. How this is worked out says it shows only in dollars.

The Federal Reserve's next household survey (expected May 2027) will supersede the 63% figure. The regions test's 12-month asOf check will fail from 22 September 2027 unless the figure is re-checked first.

EUR-Lex returned empty pages to the fetcher, so the Europe wording was confirmed through the document's indexed text and the Eurobarometer listing. The content-reviewer should open COM(2025) 681 in a browser before shipping. Separately, the Europe edition front's 49% stat label in regions.ts leaves out 'without borrowing'. That is outside this tool, but it is the same gap B found in whyItHelps.
Amounts are counted in whole cents, so a per-payday amount under half a cent counts as 0 and shows the no-amount state. This is harmless, but it is not an error message.
The three lesson files may carry uncommitted edits on this branch (the registry notes this). Change only the `tool` and `moreTools` lines.
Nothing in the tool names where to keep a buffer, and no product, bank or app appears. The link to Savings growth adds an example rate the reader types, never a promised one.

revised.title: Card balance at the minimum payment
revised.answers: If I pay only the minimum, how long does my card take to clear, and what does it cost?
revised.short: How long does the minimum take?
revised.intro: Answers one question: paying only the minimum, how many months until the balance is gone, and how much of what you pay is interest?

inputs.label: India: 'What you owe on the card'. US: 'Statement balance'. The per-edition labels live in regions.ts cardMinimum.labels.
inputs.hint: India: 'The total amount due on the statement. The run assumes nothing new goes on the card.' US: 'What the statement says you owe. The run assumes nothing new goes on the card.'
inputs.source: Example: the statements in in/protect-your-money/cost-of-borrowing (₹20,000) and us/money-basics/credit-file ($400)
inputs.validation: Required. Blank (detected on the raw string before toNumber), 0 or negative: 'Enter what you owe, more than 0.' Above 1,000,000,000 (printed with number() in the edition's grouping, so 1,00,00,00,000 in India): 'Enter an amount up to 1,000,000,000.' Any error sets aria-invalid, ties the text with aria-describedby, shows '—' in the Figure and hides both ledgers, the compare sentence and the schedule.

inputs.label: India: 'Interest rate, % a year'. US: 'Purchase APR, % a year'.
inputs.hint: India: 'Cards often print a monthly rate: 3.5% a month is 42% a year (3.5 × 12). This is the lesson's example; your card prints its own.' US: '27.5% is the CFPB's average for new general purpose card accounts opened in 2024 (report of December 2025, p.5), used here as an example. Your statement prints your own.'
inputs.source: India: the lesson's example statement (rule in.aprExample). US: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, December 2025, p.5 (rule us.aprExample)
inputs.validation: Required, 0 to 200, read to two decimal places (basis points). Blank or negative: 'Enter the yearly rate, 0 or more.' Above 200: 'Enter a yearly rate up to 200%.' 0 is allowed and removes the interest line from the run ledger.

inputs.label: India: 'Minimum due, % of what you owe'. US: 'Minimum: the month's interest plus this % of the balance'. The rule type ('percent' or 'interest-plus') comes from the edition's regions.ts entry, never from this field or the link.
inputs.hint: India: 'Each card's terms set the rule; 5% is the lesson's example. RBI's card rules say the minimum must be set so the balance does not grow.' US: 'Most cards set the minimum at 1% of the balance plus the month's interest and fees (CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, December 2025, p.70). This one is an example; your card agreement states yours.'
inputs.source: India: the lesson's 5% (rule in.minPercentExample) and RBI Directions 2025 para 23(2) (rule in.minimumMustNotGrow). US: CFPB report December 2025, p.70 (rule us.minPercentCommon)
inputs.validation: Required, above 0 and up to 100, two decimals. Blank, 0 or negative: 'Enter the minimum as a percentage, more than 0.' Above 100: 'Enter a percentage up to 100.'

inputs.label: Smallest minimum
inputs.hint: India: 'The minimum never drops below this until the last payment. An example; your card's terms print their own.' US: 'This card's floor is $25, from the lesson's statement. In 2025 card agreements floors ran from $15 to $50, most often $40 (same report, p.70).'
inputs.source: India: a made-up example, labelled as one. US: the lesson's $25 (rule us.minFloorExample), with the CFPB p.70 range and the $40 most common floor (rule us.minFloorCommon)
inputs.validation: Required, at least 1 and up to 1,000,000,000. Blank or below 1: India 'Enter the smallest minimum on your statement, at least ₹1.' US 'Enter the smallest minimum on your statement, at least $1.' A floor of 0 is refused because a percentage rule with no floor shrinks at paise level for centuries.

inputs.label: A fixed amount each month, to set beside it
inputs.hint: India: '₹1,000 is this month's minimum, kept the same every month. Leave it blank to hide this line.' US: 'An example amount. Leave it blank to hide this line.'
inputs.source: India: the lesson's ₹1,000 minimum held flat. US: example
inputs.validation: Optional. Blank (raw string empty, including '#compare=' from a link) hides the compare sentence and runs nothing. Negative: 'Enter an amount, 0 or more, or leave it blank.' Above 1,000,000,000: the balance cap message. 0 is accepted and reads as below the minimum due in month 1. An error here hides only the compare sentence; the minimum run still shows.

rules.label: The minimum amount due must be set so that paying it does not make the balance grow (no negative amortisation). Used only in India's 'grows' sentence; a minimum that just covers the interest ('flat') is not described as against the rule.
rules.sourceTitle: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, para 23(2), 28 November 2025 (replaces the 2022 Master Direction, id=12300, repealed by para 93; the NBFC credit card directions of the same date carry the same rule)

rules.label: The interest-free credit period is suspended while any balance of the previous bill is outstanding, so only month one of a run can be interest-free (a statement paid in full in month one carries no interest; later months do).
rules.sourceTitle: RBI Directions 2025 (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards), para 23(3), 28 November 2025

rules.label: Real cards levy interest only on the outstanding amount, adjusted for payments. The tool's whole-statement interest is the lesson's simplification, and How this is worked out says so.
rules.sourceTitle: RBI Directions 2025 (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards), para 23(6), 28 November 2025

rules.label: Card interest is outside GST's exemption for loan interest, so GST is charged on it. Not included in any figure (value 0 = not modelled); the assumption line says so.
rules.sourceTitle: CBIC, Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), 28 June 2017, as amended, entry 27(a): interest is exempt 'other than interest involved in credit card services'

rules.label: Example yearly rate: 3.5% a month × 12, the lesson's statement, labelled as an example in the hint
rules.sourceTitle: Business Lab lesson, Every loan as a yearly rate: apps and cards (India, reviewed 22 September 2026)

rules.label: Example minimum: 5% of what you owe, the lesson's statement
rules.sourceTitle: Business Lab lesson, Every loan as a yearly rate: apps and cards (India, reviewed 22 September 2026)

rules.label: Example APR: the average APR for new general purpose card accounts opened in 2024
rules.sourceTitle: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, report to Congress, December 2025, p.5

rules.label: Most issuers set the minimum at 1% of the balance, then add finance charges, fees and past-due amounts (the tool adds the month's interest only)
rules.sourceTitle: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, December 2025, p.70, section 4.1.1

rules.label: Minimum-payment floors in 2025 card agreements ran from $15 to $50; $40 was the most common
rules.sourceTitle: CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, December 2025, p.70, section 4.1.1

rules.label: The $25 minimum on the lesson's $400 first statement
rules.sourceTitle: Business Lab lesson, Starting a credit file without paying interest (US, reviewed 22 September 2026)

rules.label: A statement's minimum-payment estimate assumes no grace period ((b)(4)(iv)) and payments credited on the last day of the cycle ((b)(4)(viii)), so it usually shows more time and interest than this tool
rules.sourceTitle: Regulation Z, Appendix M1 to Part 1026, Repayment disclosures (CFPB eRegulations)

rules.label: The statement box gives the time in months under 2 years, otherwise rounded to whole years, for the balance on that statement
rules.sourceTitle: Regulation Z §1026.7(b)(12)(i)(B) and (D), Repayment disclosures (CFPB eRegulations)

rules.label: Grace periods are not required but most cards give one on purchases; missing a full payment loses it for that month and the next. Used in the 'paid in full' fact
rules.sourceTitle: CFPB, What is a grace period and how does it work? (last reviewed 23 September 2024)

outputs: Headline (Figure): the months to clear, paying only the minimum, as '{months} months' (number() in the edition locale), with the label 'paying only the minimum: {formatDuration(months)}'. India '142 months' / '11 years 10 months'; US '20 months' / '1 year 8 months'. Grows or flat: value '—', label 'the balance does not fall on this rule'. Over 1,200 months: value 'Over 100 years', label 'to clear it paying only the minimum'. Invalid inputs: '—'. No is-loss styling on any figure: nothing here is framed as alarm.

Ledger, month one, the statement line by line, every figure to 2 decimals (cash-book style). India (interestBase 'statement'): Owed now ₹20,000.00; + Interest for the month ₹700.00; − Minimum paid ₹1,000.00; double-ruled Owed next month ₹19,700.00 (the lesson's situation). US (interestBase 'carried'): Statement balance $400.00; − Minimum paid $25.00; = Carried $375.00; + Interest on what carried $8.59; double-ruled Next statement $383.59. When month one pays the whole statement (balance at or below the floor), the payment row reads 'Whole statement paid' and interest is 0.00. Shown whenever the inputs are valid, including the grows and flat cases (India 3.5%: ₹700 in, ₹700 out, ₹20,000 next).

Ledger, the whole run at the minimum (only when months is set): Owed now {balance}; + Interest over {formatDuration} {interest}; double-ruled Total paid {total}. India ₹20,000.00 + ₹40,332.68 = ₹60,332.68. US $400.00 + $89.79 = $489.79. At APR 0 the interest row is left out and Total paid equals the balance.
Compare sentence (when the compare field is not blank and valid), branches in the resultSentence field. India ₹1,000: 35 months (2 years 11 months), ₹14,997.77. US $50: 9 months, $35.97.

Fact, always shown, per edition. India: 'Paid in full by the due date, with nothing left from the bill before, the purchases on a statement usually carry no interest.' linked to RBI Directions 2025 para 23(3). US: 'Paid in full by the due date, with nothing carried from the statement before, the purchases on a statement usually carry no interest.' linked to the CFPB grace-period page.

Year by year, in a details fold (only when the run completes in more than one month): Year | Paid that year | Of which interest | Still owed, a table with a caption and th scope, as LoanEmi does. India 12 rows, year 1 ₹11,057.88 / ₹7,740.52 / ₹16,682.64, year 12 ₹1,896.88 / ₹306.68 / ₹0.00. US 2 rows: $300.00 / $76.30 / $176.30, then $189.79 / $13.49 / $0.00.

Assumption line under the results, per edition. India: 'Assumes nothing new goes on the card, no fees or late charges, and the same rate throughout. Interest here is the monthly rate on the whole statement, as in the lesson; cards work it out day by day on what is still owed, so a real statement will differ. Card interest also carries GST, which is not included.' US: 'Assumes nothing new goes on the card, no fees or late charges, and the same APR throughout. Interest here is worked out once a month on what carries after the payment, as in the lesson. The minimum-payment box on your statement is worked as if there were no grace period and each payment arrived at the end of the cycle, so it usually shows more time and more interest than this.'

RulesLine (src/components/RulesLine.astro) under the tool in both editions: 'Rules as of 22 September 2026:' then each sourced rule with its link and date (India: RBI Directions 2025 paras 23(2), 23(3), 23(6); CBIC 12/2017 entry 27(a). US: CFPB report pp.5 and 70; Regulation Z §1026.7(b)(12) and Appendix M1; CFPB grace periods).
No currency picker on this page: every figure is in the edition's own currency (₹ on /in, $ on /us), because the floor, the hints, the rule and the sources belong to that edition.
revised.resultSentence: Branches, first match wins, in a p.plain under the ledgers. {duration} and {cDuration} come from formatDuration; money in the sentence uses exact() (decimals only when there are any). (1) Any of balance, apr, minPercent, minFloor invalid: 'Enter what you owe, the rate, the minimum rule and the smallest minimum to see how long the minimum takes.' (2) months = 1 and interest 0: 'The minimum here covers the whole {balance}, so it is paid in one go by the due date, with no interest.' (3) Completed, APR above 0: 'Paying only the minimum clears {balance} in {duration} and adds {interest} of interest, {total} in all.' (4) Completed, APR 0: 'Paying only the minimum clears {balance} in {duration}. At 0% nothing is added.' (5) reason 'grows', India: 'On this rule the balance grows every month. RBI's card rules say the minimum amount due must be set so the balance does not grow, so check the rule printed on your statement.' (6) reason 'flat', India: 'On this rule the minimum only covers the interest, so the balance stays where it is. Check the rule printed on your statement.' (7) reason 'grows' or 'flat', US (unreachable with validation, kept as a guard): 'On these figures the balance does not fall. Check the minimum-payment rule in your card agreement and the box on your statement.' (8) reason 'over-100-years': 'Paying only the minimum, {balance} takes more than 100 years to clear on these figures.' Then, when compare is not blank and valid, one compare sentence: (a) belowMinAt = 1: 'A fixed {compare} is below this month's minimum due, so it would not count as on time.' (b) belowMinAt = n ≥ 2: 'A fixed {compare} is below the minimum due from month {n}, so from then it would not count as on time.' (c) compare run 'grows' or 'flat': 'At a fixed {compare} a month the balance does not fall.' (d) compare run 'over-100-years': 'At a fixed {compare} a month it takes more than 100 years.' (e) compare run 1 month with no interest: 'At a fixed {compare} the whole statement is paid by the due date, with no interest.' (f) completed, interest above 0: 'At a fixed {compare} a month it clears in {cDuration} and adds {cInterest}.' (g) completed at APR 0: 'At a fixed {compare} a month it clears in {cDuration}, with nothing added.' Examples. India default: 'Paying only the minimum clears ₹20,000 in 11 years 10 months and adds ₹40,332.68 of interest, ₹60,332.68 in all. At a fixed ₹1,000 a month it clears in 2 years 11 months and adds ₹14,997.77.' US default: 'Paying only the minimum clears $400 in 1 year 8 months and adds $89.79 of interest, $489.79 in all. At a fixed $50 a month it clears in 9 months and adds $35.97.' US $1,000 with a fixed $30: '… A fixed $30 is below the minimum due from month 2, so from then it would not count as on time.' No sentence says to pay more, pay less, or change card.
revised.maths:
All money inside the run is integer cents (paise) and every rate is integer basis points; each division rounds half up with an integer helper, so no float product decides a half-cent (the P6 slip: 9,900 × (27.5 / 1200) is 226.87499999999997 in floats). Shared helpers exported from src/lib/finance.ts: toCents(x) = Math.round(x × 100); fromCents(c) = c / 100; toBasisPoints(p) = Math.round(p × 100); divRoundHalfUp(n, d) for integers n ≥ 0, d > 0: q = Math.floor(n / d), rem = n − q × d, return rem × 2 ≥ d ? q + 1 : q; roundMoney(x) = Math.round(x × 100) / 100 for callers outside cent arithmetic (deductions() switches to it; lesson-math's private round2 is replaced by it). Validation caps (balance and floor ≤ 1,000,000,000, APR ≤ 200, minPercent ≤ 100) keep every product under 2^53 (1e11 cents × 20,000 bp = 2e15).

minimumRun(input: { balance: number; aprPercent: number; rule: 'percent' | 'interest-plus'; minPercent: number; minFloor: number; interestBase: 'statement' | 'carried'; fixed?: number; maxMonths?: number /* default 1200 */ }): { months: number | null; reason?: 'grows' | 'flat' | 'over-100-years'; totalInterest: number; totalPaid: number; first: { owed: number; interest: number; minimumDue: number; payment: number; carried: number; next: number }; belowMinAt: number | null; years: ScheduleYear[] }.

Set b = toCents(balance), aprBp = toBasisPoints(aprPercent), minBp = toBasisPoints(minPercent), floor = toCents(minFloor), f = fixed === undefined ? undefined : toCents(fixed), lastI = 0, stalls = 0, belowMinAt = null. For month = 1 … maxMonths:
 pct = divRoundHalfUp(b × minBp, 10000); ruleMin = rule === 'percent' ? pct : lastI + pct; required = max(ruleMin, floor).
 interestBase 'statement' (India, the lesson's model: the month's interest is the monthly rate on the whole statement balance, ₹700 on ₹20,000): if month === 1 and (f ?? required) ≥ b, the statement is paid in full by the due date, so i = 0, pay = b, minimumDue = min(required, b). Otherwise i = divRoundHalfUp(b × aprBp, 120000); due = b + i; minimumDue = min(required, due); pay = min(f ?? required, due). carried = max(b − pay, 0); next = b + i − pay.
 interestBase 'carried' (US, the lesson's model: the first statement has no interest, and what is left after the payment is charged for the month): minimumDue = min(required, b); pay = min(f ?? required, b); carried = b − pay; i = divRoundHalfUp(carried × aprBp, 120000); next = carried + i.
 If f !== undefined and belowMinAt === null and f < minimumDue, belowMinAt = month (checked every month, not just the first). Keep month 1 as first (via fromCents). Add i and pay to the totals and to the current year's block.
 If next ≤ 0: push { year: ceil(month / 12), paid, interest, balance: 0 } and return months = month.
 stalls = next ≥ b ? stalls + 1 : 0. If stalls === 2, return months null with reason next > b ? 'grows' : 'flat'. (Two statements in a row that do not fall. One rise is allowed because a US month one has no interest in its minimum: $10,000 rises to $10,126.88, then falls. Once a run stops falling it never falls again under either rule or a fixed amount, so two is enough.)
 If month % 12 === 0, push { year: month / 12, paid, interest, balance: next } and reset the block. lastI = i; b = next.
After maxMonths: months null, reason 'over-100-years'. Totals come back via fromCents; whenever months is set, totalPaid = balance + totalInterest exactly and the year rows sum to the totals.

Edge cases. A balance at or below the floor, or a fixed amount at or above the balance: 1 month, 0 interest in both bases (the P3 fix; matches the always-shown 'paid in full' fact). APR 0: no interest; months from the rule alone (India 52, US 16). A US interest-plus rule with minPercent > 0 always falls from month 2 ((carried − p·b)(1 + r) < carried(1 + r)), so on /us only a fixed amount can stall. Invalid inputs never reach minimumRun: the island shows errors instead. The rule and interestBase come only from the page's edition entry in regions.ts.

formatDuration(months: number): string, in src/lib/format.ts: y = floor(m / 12), r = m % 12; if y = 0 return r = 1 ? '1 month' : '{r} months'; if r = 0 return y = 1 ? '1 year' : '{y} years'; otherwise both parts joined by a space, singular at 1.

Island src/islands/CardMinimum.tsx: useFields('cm', numeric defaults); detects blanks on the raw strings; runs minimumRun once for the minimum (no fixed) and once with fixed = compare when compare is valid and not blank. Both runs are at most 1,200 iterations, so the result updates live on each input.

revised.howItWorks:
Each month the tool works out the minimum from the rule, takes the payment off, adds the month's interest and carries what is left to the next statement, until nothing is owed. Every amount is rounded to the paisa or cent at each step, half up, and the last payment is whatever is left.

India. Minimum = the larger of {minPercent}% of what you owe and the smallest minimum. Interest for the month = what you owe × (the yearly rate ÷ 12), on the whole statement, as the lesson's ₹20,000 statement does (₹700 at 3.5% a month). Owed next month = owed + interest − payment. This is the lesson's simplification, not how a card charges. Cards charge interest only on what is still owed after payments (RBI Directions 2025, para 23(6)), day by day, and from the date of each purchase once a bill is carried. Card interest also carries GST (CBIC Notification 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entry 27(a)), which is left out here. So a real statement will differ. A statement paid in full by the due date in month one carries no interest. After that a balance is being carried, and the interest-free period is suspended (para 23(3)). RBI's rules say the minimum amount due must be set so the balance does not grow (para 23(2)).

United States. Minimum = the larger of (last statement's interest + {minPercent}% of the balance) and the smallest minimum. Most cards set it at 1% plus interest and fees, and floors in 2025 agreements ran from $15 to $50 (CFPB, The Consumer Credit Card Market, December 2025, p.70). As in the lesson, the first statement has no interest. What is left after each payment is charged the APR ÷ 12 for the month. Your statement's minimum-payment box (Regulation Z §1026.7(b)(12)) is worked as if there were no grace period and each payment arrived on the last day of the cycle (Appendix M1). It also shows whole years once the time passes two years. So it usually shows more time and more interest than this: worked that way, the $400 statement takes 21 months and $104.02, against 20 months and $89.79 here.

Both editions. Nothing new goes on the card. No annual fee, late charge, cash advance or promotional rate is added. The rate never changes, and every payment is on time. If the balance does not fall for two statements in a row, the tool says so instead of giving a count. Past 1,200 months it says more than 100 years. The fixed amount is checked against every month's minimum, not just the first. The rule, the floor and the rate are examples: your card agreement and statement give your own.

whyItHelps (skeptic 1 fix 4; the output schema has no field for it, so the correction is recorded here): 'RBI requires a general warning on every Indian statement. A US statement's minimum-payment box gives months and total cost for that statement's balance (Regulation Z §1026.7(b)(12)), but only at the card's own rate and rule. Neither lets the reader change the rule or set a fixed amount beside it, month by month.' The false claim that neither warning uses the reader's numbers is dropped.

US statement box (skeptic 1 fix 5): the lesson's 'carried' model is kept, and How this is worked out plus the US assumption line disclose Appendix M1's no-grace, end-of-cycle assumptions ((b)(4)(iv) and (viii), opened 22 Sep 2026) and the rounding to whole years from two years. India interest model (skeptic 1 fix 6): the model is described as the lesson's simplification, citing para 23(6), and never as how Indian cards charge.

Paid in full in month one (skeptic 1 fix 7, skeptic 2 P3): in statement mode a month-one payment of at least the balance means no interest and a 1-month run. Later months keep interest (para 23(3)). Pins: ₹20,000 fixed gives 1 month and 0 interest; ₹150 gives 1 month, ₹150 paid, 0 interest. The same holds in the US carried mode ($20, or $400 fixed).

Never-falls wording (skeptic 1 fix 8, skeptic 2 P2): skeptic 2's per-reason copy is used. Skeptic 1's India sentence ('RBI's card rules require the minimum amount due to be set so this cannot happen') is rejected for the flat case, because 23(2) bars a growing balance, not a flat one, and the tool's own 3.5% pin is flat. India 'grows' cites RBI, India 'flat' makes no RBI claim, and the US has its own wording. With validation (minPercent > 0) the US interest-plus minimum always falls from month 2, so on /us only a fixed amount can stall.

US sources (skeptic 1 fix 9): the minPercent and minFloor hints now cite the CFPB report. Checked in the PDF on 22 Sep 2026: p.70 says most issuers use 1% of the balance plus finance charges, and 2025 floors ran from $15 to $50, most often $40. p.5 gives the 27.5% average for new accounts opened in 2024. These are added as dated rules.
Optional per-edition config (skeptic 1 fix 10, skeptic 2 P11): cardMinimum is optional on ToolDefaults. [tool].astro guards the island and fails the build if a listed edition lacks defaults.

Validation (skeptic 2 P5): balance > 0 and ≤ 1,000,000,000; the floor at least 1 (a 0 floor produced false never-falls results at paise level, even at 0%); APR 0 to 200; minPercent above 0 up to 100; compare 0 or more, blank to hide. Any core field error gives the Figure '—' and hides the ledgers. Balance 0 is refused, so 'clears ₹0 in 0 months' cannot occur, and the cap stops a 20-digit link value.

Durations (skeptic 2 P7): formatDuration fixes '1 years 8 months', '0 years 9 months' and '3 years 0 months'. The Figure keeps '{n} months', so the e2e pins '142 months' and '20 months' hold, and it adds the duration as its label.

Assumptions (skeptic 2 P8), applied in part. The assumption lines now say interest is worked once a month on one figure and that real cards work day by day. India's GST line now has a dated official source (CBIC Notification 12/2017-CT(Rate) entry 27(a), opened 22 Sep 2026), but GST stays out of the maths because no rate source was added. Rejected: labelling the interest line 'Interest, at least', and saying 'the real figures are higher' for India. The lesson's model charges interest on the whole statement even after a payment, which 23(6) says real cards do not, so the model is not a guaranteed floor there. India says 'a real statement will differ'. The US keeps 'usually shows more', which Appendix M1 and the CFPB p.76 example both support.

'Paid in full' fact (skeptic 2 P9): reworded to 'with nothing left from the bill before' (India) and 'with nothing carried from the statement before' (US), linked to RBI Directions 2025 para 23(3) and to the CFPB grace-period page (last reviewed 23 Sep 2024, which says a missed full payment loses the grace period for that month and the next).

Page labelling (skeptic 2 P10), applied in part. The Practice/Calculator label now comes from tool.format, and the per-edition scenario strings are wired in. Rejected: deriving regionSub from the tool's kind, because the edition menu must depend on whether the target edition has the tool. Replaced with a per-edition `subs` map: India and US keep the tool page, Europe gets /eu/tools.

Lesson links (skeptic 2 P11 and the registry): the registry's 'us/credit-file: tool: card-minimum' is rejected. Both linked lessons have loan explorables that hand off through `tool` (toolHref = d.tool ?? 'loan'), so `tool` stays loan and card-minimum goes in moreTools in both lessons.

Currency picker removed from this tool (task rule): every edition-bound rule, label and copy arrives as props from the page's edition, money is formatted in region.locale, and lp:locale is neither read nor written, so a stored en-US preference cannot put RBI copy in dollars. The link carries only numbers after the #.

Kept as they were: the 10 original default pins (India 142 / 40,332.68 / 60,332.68, 700 + 300 → 19,700, fixed 1,000 → 35 / 14,997.77, 3.5% and 3% never fall, APR 0 → 52; US 20 / 89.79 / 489.79, 375 / 8.59 / 383.59, fixed 50 → 9 / 35.97), all recomputed in node with the integer-cent algorithm. The US default of $400 and $25 and the 27.5% sentence on CFPB p.5 were re-checked. Europe stays deferred.
risks: The model is the lessons' model, not a card's. India charges the month's interest on the whole statement and leaves out GST; the US charges only what carries after the payment. Real statements differ, and the page says so in the assumption line, in How this is worked out, and with the statement-box comparison pinned (21 months and $104.02 against 20 and $89.79).

Sources that go stale: the CFPB figures describe 2025 agreements and 2024 accounts, and the RBI Directions and CBIC notification are amended from time to time. Every rule carries an asOf, and the regions test fails after 12 months. content-reviewer should confirm that CBIC 12/2017 entry 27(a) still reads the same in the current consolidated notification, and add the RBI NBFC credit card directions' own URL if a reader asks about NBFC cards.

Fear framing: a card run can reach decades (US $10,000 at the minimum takes 304 months). The Figure has no loss styling, the sentence states months and money flatly, the 'paid in full' fact is always shown, and the never-falls lines point to the reader's own statement rather than warning.

Advice: the tool never says to pay more, to switch cards or to transfer a balance. The compare amount is the reader's own number. The India lesson's takeaway 'pay as far above the minimum as you can' stays in the lesson and is not repeated on the tool.
Accuracy: integer-cent arithmetic changes three skeptic pins by 2–5 cents against float runs. The unit tests pin the integer results, and reviewers should not 'fix' them back to the float figures.
Lesson hand-off depends on foundation work: until moreTools and the LessonLayout link land, neither linked lesson links to card-minimum. The e2e test should cover the link from both lessons.

Removing the currency picker on this tool departs from the kit's usual behaviour. The one e2e currency test is on break-even and stays. The CLAUDE.md 'current state' line should say that tools with edition rules show no currency field.
Europe readers who switch edition from a card-minimum page land on /eu/tools, which has no card tool (no EU lesson teaches revolving balances). This is intended and is covered by the e2e test.

revised.title: Pay-later plans against one payday
revised.answers: What is left of this pay once my pay-later plans take their share before the next payday?
revised.short: What do my pay-later plans leave?
revised.intro: Answers one question: after living costs and every pay-later payment due before your next pay, what is left of this pay?

inputs.label: Pay arriving this payday
inputs.hint: What reaches your account from this pay, after deductions: your net or take-home pay.
inputs.source: example: the worked deduction in eu/credit-and-fraud/bnpl-is-credit (start 1200, 'Net pay') and us/how-business-works/bnpl (start 1317, 'Take-home pay')
inputs.validation: Read with readField(text): '' gives null, otherwise Number(text); never toNumber(), which keeps a '-' and turns '1e3' into 13. Blank or 0: no error; the ledger and facts are hidden and the sentence asks for the pay (status 'no-pay'). NaN: 'Enter a number.' Below 0: 'Pay cannot be below 0.' Above 10,000,000: 'Enter an amount up to 10,000,000.' Error text sits under the field, tied with aria-describedby, with aria-invalid on the input; any error sets status 'invalid' and hides every figure. Stored to whole cents.

inputs.label: Living costs until your next pay
inputs.hint: Rent, bills, food, transport and phone: what this pay has to cover before the next one arrives.
inputs.source: example: the same two worked deductions (EU 'Rent and living costs' 804; US 'Rent, bills and food' 817)
inputs.validation: Blank counts as 0 with no error. NaN: 'Enter a number.' Below 0: 'Living costs cannot be below 0.' Above 10,000,000: 'Enter an amount up to 10,000,000.' Any error sets status 'invalid'.

inputs.label: Moved to savings from this pay
inputs.hint: Leave at 0 if nothing moves.
inputs.source: example: us/how-business-works/bnpl worked line 'Savings' 132; the EU lesson moves nothing
inputs.validation: Blank counts as 0 with no error. NaN: 'Enter a number.' Below 0: 'Savings cannot be below 0.' Above 10,000,000: 'Enter an amount up to 10,000,000.' Any error sets status 'invalid'. At 0 the savings ledger line and its subtotal are not shown.

inputs.label: Pay-later payments due before your next pay

defaults.eu: 30~2~4~1|36~2~4~1|24~2~4~1 (three plans: 30, 36 and 24, each payment 2 of 4, 1 due before the next pay)
defaults.us: 15~2~4~1|15~2~4~1|15~2~4~1 (three plans of 15, each payment 2 of 4, 1 due before the next pay)

inputs.hint: Every payment that leaves before your next pay arrives, not only those due on payday. Plans are numbered Plan 1 to Plan 8: no shop or lender names.
inputs.source: example: the lessons' app screens (trainers, coat, books; headphones, jacket, shoes), each on 'Payment 2 of 4'; the EU plans and pay are monthly, the US plans and pay every two weeks, so 1 payment of each falls before the next pay
inputs.validation: 0 to 8 rows (MAX_PLAN_ROWS = 8, exported from src/lib/plans-link.ts and shared by the island and the codec). Each row is a fieldset whose legend is 'Plan n'; there is no name field, so no free text exists to store or link. At 8 rows 'Add a plan' is disabled and this visible text follows it, tied with aria-describedby: 'This tool holds up to 8 plans. Any more are left out of these totals, so the plans would take more than shown.' Nothing tells the reader to move plans into living costs. Removing every row is allowed (status 'no-plans').

inputs.label: Payment amount
inputs.hint: One payment, as the plan shows it.
inputs.source: example: the lessons' screens (€30, €36, €24; $15 three times)
inputs.validation: Blank or 0: the row stays in the ledger as 'Plan n' at 0, is not checked further and is not counted. NaN: 'Enter a number.' Below 0: 'A payment cannot be below 0.' Above 10,000,000: 'Enter an amount up to 10,000,000.'

inputs.label: Payment number
inputs.hint: As the plan shows it: for 'payment 2 of 4', 2 here and 4 in the next box.
inputs.source: example: 'Payment 2 of 4' on both lessons' screens
inputs.validation: Checked only when the row's amount is above 0. Blank: 'Enter the payment number and the total as the plan shows them, for example payment 2 of 4.' Not a whole number, below 1, or higher than the total: 'Payment number must be a whole number, no higher than the total.' inputMode numeric, step 1, min 1, max 48.

inputs.label: Out of how many
inputs.hint: The total number of payments on the plan.
inputs.source: example: 'of 4' on both lessons' screens
inputs.validation: Checked only when the row's amount is above 0. Blank: the same message as the payment number. Not a whole number, below 1 or above 48: 'A plan here can have from 1 to 48 payments.' The visible label 'Out of how many' is the start of its accessible name (WCAG 2.5.3).

inputs.label: Payments due before your next pay
inputs.hint: Counting the one due on this payday. A plan paid every two weeks, against pay that arrives monthly, has 2 or 3.

(2) no-pay (pay blank or 0): 'Enter the pay arriving this payday to see what is left.' (3) short-before-plans (pay − living − savings < 0): with savings = 0, 'Living costs of {living} are {gap} more than this pay of {pay}, before any plan.'; with savings > 0, 'Living costs and savings come to {living + savings}, {gap} more than this pay of {pay}, before any plan.'; when count > 0 add ' On top of that, {take} {plansTotal}.' revised.maths: paydayAfterPlans(input: { pay: number | null; living: number | null; savings: number | null; plans: { amount: number | null; k: number | null; n: number | null; d: number | null }[] }): PaydayResult, a pure function in src/lib/finance.ts. The island turns each field's text into number | null with readField(text) = text.trim() === '' ? null : Number(text); NaN is kept so it can be reported. Constants: MAX_MONEY = 10,000,000; MAX_PAYMENTS = 48; MAX_DUE = 4; MAX_PLAN_ROWS = 8 (imported from plans-link.ts). (1) Validation, before any arithmetic, into errors: Record<string, ErrorCode> keyed 'pay', 'living', 'savings', 'plans.{i}.amount', 'plans.{i}.k', 'plans.{i}.n', 'plans.{i}.d'. Money fields: null counts as 0 (pay null or 0 gives status 'no-pay'); NaN gives 'nan'; below 0 gives 'below-zero'; above MAX_MONEY gives 'too-big'. Only the first 8 rows are read. For a row whose amount is above 0: k and n must be integers with 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 48 (blank gives 'k-of-n-missing', otherwise 'k-of-n'); d must be an integer from 1 to 4 ('due'); k + d − 1 ≤ n ('due-too-many', message uses n − k + 1). A row whose amount is 0 or blank is not checked and not counted. Any error returns { status: 'invalid', errors } and no figures. (2) Arithmetic in integer cents through shared helpers exported from finance.ts: toCents(v) = Math.round(v × 100), fromCents(c) = c / 100, roundMoney(v) = fromCents(toCents(v)); lesson-math.ts drops its private round2 and imports roundMoney. afterLiving = pay − living; beforePlans = afterLiving − savings; per counted row: taken = a × d, owedIncluding = a × (n − k + 1), owedAfter = a × (n − k − d + 1); plansTotal = Σ taken; left = beforePlans − plansTotal; count = Σ d over counted rows; plansCounted = number of counted rows. share = plansTotal / pay as an unrounded ratio (never round1 then '%'); the island writes it with percent(share, locale, 1). owedIncluding and owedAfter assume each remaining payment equals this one, as in the usual split into four. (3) status: 'short-before-plans' if beforePlans < 0; else 'no-plans' if count = 0; else 'short-after-plans' if left < 0; else 'ok'. lastPayments = count > 0 and owedAfter = 0. (4) Returns { status, pay, living, savings, afterLiving, beforePlans, lines: { label, amount }[], plansTotal, left, count, plansCounted, share, owedIncluding, owedAfter, lastPayments }, all money as fromCents values. lines keeps every read row in order: label 'Plan {i+1}', or 'Plan {i+1}, {d} payments' when a counted row has d > 1; a row at 0 keeps 'Plan {i+1}' with amount 0. DeductionLine and deductions() are unchanged: the subtotal labels are drawn by the island ('Left after living costs' after the living-costs line always; 'Left after living costs and savings' after the savings line, which appears only when savings > 0) with a new Result subtotal prop; for the defaults the running figures equal deductions() exactly (pinned). Edge cases: pay 0 or blank → 'no-pay', share hidden; no rows or only zero rows → 'no-plans'; living plus savings above pay → 'short-before-plans' (the plans are not blamed); every counted plan on its last payments → owedAfter 0 and the sentence says nothing is owed after them; left exactly 0 → 'nothing is left'; amounts with cents never drift (100 − 33.33 × 3 = 0.01, where plain floats give 0.010000000000005116). Plans that charge interest, whose last payment differs, or whose dates were moved are not modelled. Codec, new src/lib/plans-link.ts beside budget-link.ts (which keeps '-' and is not copied): encodePlans(rows) writes 'a~k~n~d' joined by '|', only for rows the decoder would accept, a blank amount written as 0, at most 8 rows. decodePlans(text): null for a non-string, an empty string or one longer than 200 characters (8 rows at the maximum are 159); split on '|', stop at 8 accepted rows; each part must split into exactly 4 on '~' and match amount /^\d{1,8}(\.\d{1,2})?$/, k and n /^\d{1,2}$/, d /^[1-4]$/, then amount ≤ 10,000,000, 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 48 and k + d − 1 ≤ n; failing rows are dropped; null when no row survives. Number() is applied only after a regex passes, so '0x1F', '1e9', 'Infinity', '-5' and '' never reach it. In a link the rows go after the # as plans=… with pay, living, savings and cur, through the kit's hash mode.

revised.howItWorks:
What is left = pay − living costs − money moved to savings − every pay-later payment due before your next pay. Each plan's line is its payment × the number of its payments due before your next pay, which you choose from 1 to 4: the tool does not know the plan's dates, so it counts payments, not days. A plan paid every two weeks against pay that arrives monthly has 2 or 3 before the next pay; one on the same schedule as your pay has 1.

Owed on the plans, counting these payments = each payment × (total payments − payment number + 1). Still owed after them = each payment × (total payments − payment number − payments due before your next pay + 1). Both assume every payment left on a plan is the same size, as in the usual split into four. A plan whose last payment is different, a plan that charges interest, or one whose dates have been moved is not worked out here; for a plan that charges interest, the loan calculator works out the monthly payment. The plans' share is what they take ÷ this pay. The tool holds up to 8 plans; any more are left out of these totals, so the plans would take more than shown. A late fee or a bank charge is not added to the sum.

The tool takes no interest rate. At 0% interest a plan charges nothing extra while every payment lands on time; what is owed is the same either way.

What this adds to the budget planner (linked): the planner takes one amount per line for a month; this counts each plan's payments before your next pay and shows what is still owed on the plans after them.

Europe: From 20 November 2026 the revised Consumer Credit Directive, Directive (EU) 2023/2225, covers most pay-later plans (European Commission, consumer credit page, linked). Each EU country's own law sets any limit on late-payment charges: the directive lets countries hold them to what a missed payment costs the lender, and a country that allows extra charges on top of that must cap them (Article 35, linked to EUR-Lex). A payment that fails can also bring a charge from your bank.

United States: The fee note's $9.70 is the 2023 average late fee at the four of six large lenders that charged one (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, The Buy Now, Pay Later Market, December 2025, Table 7, linked), not any plan's fee. Some states limit these fees, so the amount can depend on where you live (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, September 2022, linked). New York proposed rules in 2026 that would limit them (Department of Financial Services, February 2026, linked); they were not in force when this was checked on 22 September 2026. Your bank can add an overdraft or non-sufficient funds fee when an automatic payment finds too little in the account.

Nothing you type leaves your browser. A copied link carries the numbers after the #, which browsers do not send to any server; anyone you send it to sees them. Reset clears them from the address bar.
