src/islands/PayLaterPayday.tsx (new, about 4 KB gz, page well under 90 KB): useFields('plp', { pay, living, savings }) plus a rows state of { id, amount, k, n, d } with a stable id counter so Preact keys never reuse the wrong row; rows start from decodePlans(readLinkParams().plans) or the defaults, and adopt values typed into server-rendered row inputs before hydration, as useFields does. Each row is a fieldset.plan-row with legend 'Plan n': NumberField 'Payment amount'; side by side 'Payment number' and 'Out of how many' (inputMode numeric, step 1); SelectField 'Payments due before your next pay'; a remove button whose visible text is 'Remove' and whose accessible name is 'Remove Plan n', at least 44px tall. Keyboard: after 'Add a plan' focus the new row's amount; after 'Remove Plan n' focus the amount of the row that takes its place, or 'Add a plan' when none follows, and set the visible role='status' line under the rows. Error text per field is tied with aria-describedby. The fee note's source link has rel='noopener noreferrer'. HowItWorks carries this spec's text with links to the budget planner and the loan calculator.
src/islands/tools.css: .plan-row (fieldset reset, border-top var(--line), a grid that stacks at 360px with the two count fields sharing one line, var(--space-*) gaps), tokens only, no inline style.

src/layouts/LessonLayout.astro: the registry's 'Your own numbers: {answers}' links after the explorable carry both BNPL lessons to this tool and to the budget planner; DeductionExplorer.tsx is not changed.

Tests: tests/e2e/tools.spec.ts, at 360 and 1280 px: /eu/tools/pay-later-payday opens on €306 and /us/tools/pay-later-payday on $323 (the double-ruled total); add a plan and remove Plan 2 with the keyboard only, checking focus and the status text; a 9th plan cannot be added and the cap note shows; typing -30 in living shows 'Living costs cannot be below 0.' and hides the figures; the # link round-trip and '#main'; the edition menu tails; axe with no serious or critical issues. scripts/js-budget.mjs keeps the page under 90 KB.
changes: S1/P1 (sentence left out savings): the sentence now names every line that came off, using the facts skeptic's wording with the amount ('After living costs, $132 to savings and 3 installments, $323 is left of $1,317.') rather than the safety skeptic's bare 'savings', so the sentence adds up by itself. Pinned for both editions.

S2/P2 (US subtotal mislabelled): the ledger shows 'Left after living costs' after the living-costs line always, and a second subtotal after the savings line when savings > 0. The two skeptics disagreed on the words. I took 'Left after living costs and savings' (facts) over 'Left after savings' (safety): in the tool the row stands alone, without the lesson's captions. P11/F11: DeductionLine is not extended. The labels come from the island through a new Result subtotal prop.

S3/P10 (hash claim untrue for the kit): tool-kit.tsx is now in scope. readLinkParams reads # first and ignores a bare fragment such as '#main'. ToolActions writes the hash and clears the query. The link carries pay, living, savings, plans and cur. Reset clears the fragment. An e2e test covers it. PROJECT_BRIEF §6 ('query string') is superseded for every tool by the registry change.

S4/P3 (schedules differ): each row now has 'Payments due before your next pay' (d). The plan line takes payment × d, and the hint reads 'Every payment that leaves before your next pay arrives, not only those due on payday' (F3's hint, without 'today's'). New pin: a monthly payer with 2 payments on each plan has €216 left.

S5 vs F3 (period wording): I took the safety fix. There is one label, 'Left until your next pay', in both editions, and 'period' is gone from regions.ts. I rejected F3's 'Paid' select (weekly to monthly, BLS default) because it changes only a label, not a figure. It would add a second question to a one-question tool, and the per-row d already carries the schedule mismatch that motivated it. The BLS figure is therefore not used.

S6 vs F3/F12 (row model): I took the safety skeptic's 'Payment k of n' as the screens print it, over the facts skeptic's 'leftAfter' count. Readers copy 'Payment 2 of 4' straight off the screen, so they no longer have to work out 4 − 2, which fixes the error-prone input. d runs 1–4 (facts) rather than 1–3 (safety): a monthly payer with weekly or 30-day plans can reach 4, and k + d − 1 ≤ n bounds it anyway. Limits are 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 48 (safety). Fields are read with Number() into readField, never toNumber(), which keeps '-' and turns '1e3' into 13. Errors hide every figure rather than treating a bad value as 0.
Money limit: the safety skeptic said 10,000,000 and the facts skeptic 1,000,000. I took 10,000,000 because a reader who switches the picker to ₦ or ₹ types much larger numbers.

S7/P12/F12 (loose codec): new plans-link.ts with strict regexes, validity checks after the regex, a 200-character cap, bad rows dropped and null when none survive. Every listed attack string is pinned. budget-link.ts is not copied.

S8 (plurals, blank rows counted): the word pair comes from regions.ts and is chosen by count. 'plan/plans' and 'it/them' follow the number of counted plans. Only rows with an amount above 0 are counted. Zero rows stay in the ledger, numbered.

S9 (shortfall blamed the plans): there are now three branches: short before any plan, short only after the plans, and no pay. Plus no plans, last payments and nothing left. None says overspent, avoid, cut, should or free.
S10 ('after today'): the owed figures and the sentence now say 'after these instalments' / 'counting these instalments', which holds whenever the tool is used.

S11 (hard-coded %, no round helpers): share is an unrounded ratio formatted with percent(…, locale, 1) (pt-BR shows 7,5%). finance.ts exports toCents/fromCents/roundMoney, and every sum is in integer cents (pin: 100 − 3 × 33.33 = 0.01 exactly).

S12/P4/P6/F4/F6 (fee): the fee is no longer a Fact row. It is a labelled note per edition, titled 'Late fee if a payment is missed', and adds that a failed payment can bring a bank charge. The US wording differs from the safety fix: its 2021 '$7 or $8' was superseded, and I verified the CFPB's December 2025 Data Spotlight (Table 7, nominal): an average $9.70 per late fee assessed in 2023 at the four of six lenders that charged them, with 4.1% of loans charged one. That report is now the rule with its source and asOf. 'CFPB' is spelled out. Europe keeps €15 only as 'the lesson's made-up example', and each country's law sets any limit.

F4 (lesson and tool should agree): the US lesson's screen goes from $7 to $10, with a 2023 hint. The details gain the 2023 figure and its source. The 2021 detail stays because it is still true of 2021.

F5/P5 (US state variation): verified on page 23 of the CFPB's September 2022 report ('Depending on the borrower's state of residence, late fees may vary'), and now in How this is worked out and the note. New York was applied only in part. The DFS press release (23 February 2026) confirms proposed rules 'limiting late fees', and the 60-day comment period after the 15 July 2026 notice ended 14 September 2026. The $8 figure appears only in secondary reports (PYMNTS citing Bloomberg Law), not on the DFS page I could open, so the tool says New York proposed limits, not yet in force when checked on 22 September 2026, without a dollar figure.

S13/P9/F9 (cap of four; 'add the rest to living costs'): raised to 8 through MAX_PLAN_ROWS, shared by the island and the codec. The living-costs advice is gone. At the cap, 'Add a plan' is disabled with visible text tied by aria-describedby. I merged the two skeptics' wordings: 'This tool holds up to 8 plans. Any more are left out of these totals, so the plans would take more than shown.'

S14 (indexed as Practice; edition menu): kind comes from the registry's tool.format, so this page is filed as 'Calculator'. RegionTabs gets a per-edition tail (subFor), so /eu/tools/pay-later-payday leads to /us/tools/pay-later-payday and /in/tools. There is an e2e test.
S15 (no scenario): regions.ts gains per-edition scenario strings with the lessons' figures and no shop or lender names. [tool].astro reads them.

S16/P13/F13 (lesson link; what this adds over the budget planner): both BNPL lessons get tool: pay-later-payday plus moreTools: [budget], so the budget planner keeps them in its list. For the hand-off I used the registry's 'Your own numbers' link, which LessonLayout renders after the explorable, instead of adding toolHref to DeductionExplorer. The result is the same (lessons without a tool get no link), with no change to the island and no extra JavaScript on lesson pages. How this is worked out says what the tool adds over the budget planner. seeAlso links the two tool pages both ways (Europe and US only).

S17/P7/F7 (whyItHelps overstated): reworded from the CFPB report of 13 January 2025, checked in the PDF: 'In 2022, about 63% of pay-in-four borrowers at six large US lenders originated more than one loan at the same time at some point, and about 37% of 18–24-year-olds with a credit record financed at least one purchase with those lenders.' It applies to the research record and any reader-facing copy.

P8/F8 (NerdWallet): the claim becomes 'found no tool that adds several pay-later plans against one payday; NerdWallet's installment-loan calculator covers one loan at a time'. modelledOn drops 'NerdWallet's small capped add another rows' and cites BudgetPlanner's rows and the two lessons' deduction explorers.

S18 (keyboard unspecified): focus after add and remove, the status text, accessible names that include the plan number, 44px targets and label-in-name for 'Out of how many' are all specified, with keyboard-only e2e at 360px.

P14/F14 (EU wording): How this is worked out now says the directive applies from 20 November 2026 and covers most pay-later plans. Each country's law sets any limit on late charges: the directive lets countries hold them to the lender's costs, and extra default charges, if allowed, must be capped (Article 35). EUR-Lex returned empty pages and a direct download was not permitted, so the Article 35 reading rests on a Chambers and Partners summary and a search excerpt of 35(3). This is listed as a risk to verify before shipping.

My own change, not from the skeptics: the headline Figure is dropped. BRAND_GUIDE §5 and DESIGN §4 keep the Figure for a count or a payment. Here the answer is the ledger's double-ruled total, as in the budget planner, so the total carries the answer and the loss style plus the word 'Short'.
Rejected in part: the safety skeptic's EU fee sentence was replaced by F6's fuller 'made-up example' wording. The two do not conflict; F6's makes the example's status explicit.
risks: The Article 35 wording (national limits on default charges, capped at the lender's costs; extra charges capped) was checked only against a Chambers and Partners summary and a search excerpt. EUR-Lex returned empty pages to WebFetch, and downloading it with curl was not permitted. Read Article 35 on EUR-Lex before shipping, and keep the sentence general if its title or numbering differs.

The US fee figure is 2023 data published in December 2025. The 12-month asOf test in the regions test will fail on 22 September 2027 if nobody re-checks it. Update it when the CFPB publishes newer figures. It is an average across four lenders, and the note says so, so it does not read as any plan's fee.

New York's rules were proposed, not final, when checked on 22 September 2026. Once they are adopted, the note is stale. Re-check the DFS site and decide whether to add the adopted cap with its own dated source.

The answer depends on the reader counting payments due before the next pay. The hint, the default of 1 and How this is worked out explain it, but a wrong count gives a wrong figure. The tool cannot see plan dates and must never ask for a lender or shop name to find them.

Tone: shortfall sentences must stay arithmetic. The content-reviewer should read every branch against LEARNING_DESIGN's no-moralising rule (SPENT) and the anti-BNPL risk. The tool neither praises nor blames 0%.

Privacy: the # keeps the numbers off every server, but anyone given the link sees them, and the fragment sits in local browser history until Reset clears it. The kit's line says the first. The security-reviewer should check readLinkParams and the codec.

Currency picker: a reader who picks another currency sees their figures in it but the fee note in the edition's currency. This is deliberate (the fee is a US or EU figure), but it can look inconsistent. Do not reword the note to follow the picker.
Rounding: a share just under 100% (for example 99.99%) is written as 100.0% by Intl. This only happens when the plans take almost the whole pay, and the ledger shows the exact figures.

The lesson edits (the US screen from $7 to $10, the new details line and source) need the content-reviewer before commit. Check the 1,250-word and hint caps in lessons.test.ts after the edit (the new hint is one word shorter).
Only the first 8 plans are counted. A reader with more sees the cap note, but the share and the owed figures understate their debt. The note says so in text.
Row values typed before hydration on a slow connection must be adopted like useFields does, or they reset. The e2e test should type before islands load.

revised.title: A loan's cost as a yearly rate
revised.answers: I get this much and pay back that much: what is that as a yearly rate?
revised.short: What is this loan as a yearly rate?
revised.intro: Answers one question: whatever the charge is called, a fee, a flat rate or 'no-cost', what does it come to over a year?

inputs.label: Amount borrowed
inputs.hint: The loan amount on the offer, or the price of what you are buying in instalments.
inputs.source: example: in/protect-your-money/cost-of-borrowing, first section ('An app taking ₹500 to lend ₹5,000 for seven days')
inputs.validation: Read with parseAmount (blank is null, not 0). Blank, 0, negative or not finite: 'Enter the amount borrowed, more than 0.' Above 1e12: 'Enter an amount of {money(1e12)} or less.' Paise beyond two places are rounded to the paisa (toCents). The error sits under the field with aria-invalid; no rate is shown while any field is in error.

inputs.label: Fees and charges at the start
inputs.hint: Processing fees, insurance and other charges collected through the lender, with the GST you pay on them, and interest taken up front. A Key Facts Statement may list fees before GST; a card's instalment plan lists them in its terms.
inputs.source: https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=12942 (third-party charges such as insurance and legal charges form part of the APR; amounts may be disclosed net of taxes such as GST; credit card receivables are exempt from the KFS)
inputs.validation: Blank counts as 0. Negative: 'Fees cannot be below 0. Type 0 if there are none.' Above 1e12: 'Enter an amount of {money(1e12)} or less.' If the fees (plus a first repayment paid on the day) take the whole amount, the fields stay valid and the results say nothing reaches you, with no rate.

inputs.label: Each repayment
inputs.hint: The one payment, or each equal instalment. For a flat-rate offer, type the instalment printed on it.
inputs.source: example: the lesson's seven-day app loan (₹5,000 plus ₹500)
inputs.validation: Blank, 0, negative or not finite: 'Enter the repayment, more than 0.' Above 1e12: 'Enter an amount of {money(1e12)} or less.' Rounded to the paisa.

inputs.label: Number of repayments
inputs.hint: Every instalment, counting one paid on the day.
inputs.source: example
inputs.validation: Blank, 0, negative, not finite, or below 1 after rounding down: 'Enter how many repayments, at least 1.' Above 600: 'This tool works up to 600 repayments.' Not whole: counted as the whole number below, with a note (not an error) under the field, tied by aria-describedby: 'Counted as {n}: repayments come whole.'

inputs.label: Length of each period
inputs.hint: For one repayment, the time until it is due. For instalments, the time from one to the next.
inputs.source: lesson method (365 ÷ 7 weeks, 12 months); the monthly × 12 convention is the RBI KFS illustration, id=12942
inputs.validation: Only 'week', 'month' or 'days' is accepted from the page, the DOM adoption or a link; anything else falls back to the default 'week'.

inputs.label: Days in each period
inputs.hint: A year counts as 365 days, so 91 days is 365 ÷ 91 periods.
inputs.source: example (matches the 7-day default, so choosing 'Another number of days' does not move the answer)
inputs.validation: Rendered and read only when period is 'days'. Blank, 0, negative, not finite, or below 1 after rounding down: 'Enter the days in each period, at least 1.' Above 3650: 'Enter 3,650 days (ten years) or fewer.' Not whole: rounded down with the note 'Counted as {d} days.'

inputs.label: First repayment
inputs.hint: Shop instalment plans often take the first part on the day. A Key Facts Statement shows when repayments start.
options: later: One period after the money arrives
on-the-day: On the day the money arrives
inputs.source: RBI KFS illustration, 'commencement of repayments, post sanction: 30 days' (id=12942)
inputs.validation: Only 'later' or 'on-the-day' is accepted; anything else falls back to 'later'. With 'on-the-day' and one repayment: error under this field, 'With one repayment made on the day, nothing is borrowed. Choose one period after, or count more repayments.'

rules.label: Periods in a year for monthly repayments. A Key Facts Statement's APR is 'computed on net disbursed amount using IRR approach and reducing balance method'; the Directions' own illustration works out as the monthly rate times 12 (₹19,600 net, 24 × ₹969.73, 1.4225% a month, 17.07%).
rules.sourceTitle: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, RBI/DOR/2025-26/362, 28 November 2025, updated as on 1 July 2026: Key Facts Statement and APR

rules.label: Days in a year when each period is counted in days: periods in a year = 365 ÷ days (the lesson's method). The Directions set no day count for APR, so a lender's APR on a loan counted in days can differ: 500.4% day by day against 521.4% here on the 7-day example.
rules.sourceTitle: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, RBI/DOR/2025-26/362, 28 November 2025, updated as on 1 July 2026 (no day-count convention stated)

rules.label: The Directions' KFS illustration, held as a unit-test pin and quoted in How this is worked out: ₹20,000 sanctioned at 15% fixed, ₹400 of fees, ₹19,600 net disbursed, 24 monthly instalments (₹970 printed, ₹969.73 unrounded), repayments starting 30 days after sanction, ₹3,274 of interest, APR 17.07%.
rules.sourceTitle: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, RBI/DOR/2025-26/362, KFS illustrative example

outputs: Headline (Figure): value '{yearly}%' (default '521.4%'), label 'a year, worked out from the figures above'. '—' in any error or no-rate state. Above 10,000 it reads 'over 10,000%'; above 0 but rounding to 0.0 it reads 'under 0.1%'.

Ledger (Result rows, in order, each row adding up to the next): 'Amount borrowed' ₹5,000; '− Fees and charges at the start' ₹0; only with first = on-the-day: '− First repayment, paid on the day' ₹4,000; subtotal (single rule) 'Reaches you' ₹5,000; the repayments row, worded by case: count 1 'Repaid after 7 days' / 'after a month' / 'after {d} days' ₹5,500; instalments 'Repaid, {n} × {repayment}, the first one period after' (first = later) or 'Repaid later, {n − 1} × {repayment}' (on the day); only when a paise gap is treated as nil: 'Rounding in the instalments' ±₹0.01; subtotal (single rule) 'Cost of borrowing' ₹500; 'Rate for the 7 days' (count 1) or 'Rate for each month, on what is still owed' (instalments) 10%; '× Periods in a year, about 52.14' with the figure '365 ÷ 7' (for a month: label '× Periods in a year', figure '12'; for days: '365 ÷ {d}', 'about {round2(365/d)}'); main (double rule) 'Yearly rate' 521.4%.
Footnote under the ledger (--text-sm, --muted): 'Rates are rounded for display; the yearly rate is the rate shown times the periods in a year.'
The one-sentence result (see resultSentence).
A plain line: 'A regulated loan's Key Facts Statement prints its APR. Set this beside it.'

RulesLine under the tool (src/components/RulesLine.astro): 'Method as of 22 September 2026: the APR on a Key Facts Statement is worked out on what reaches you, as a monthly rate times 12 (Reserve Bank of India, Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, updated 1 July 2026).'

How this is worked out (details fold): the method text in howItWorks; for instalments (not capped), the repayment table 'Repayment by repayment' with columns Repayment | Paid | Charge for the period | Paid off | Still owed, one row per repayment up to 60, grouped in twelves above 60 (rows '1–12' …), ending at ₹0, with a first row 'On the day' when first = on-the-day; and the compounded figure line 'If the same charge is paid period after period, it compounds to {compounded}% over a year' (default 'over 10,000%', the phone plan 36.2%). The word 'effective' is never used for any figure of the tool's own.
revised.resultSentence:
Branches, first match wins. {money} values use the edition's locale; {rate} is the period rate as shown (trailing zeros trimmed); {yearly} is yearlyShown or 'over 10,000%' / 'under 0.1%'. Period words: week → {after}='after 7 days', {forSpan}='for the 7 days', {cadence}='one each week', {perUnit}='a week'; month → 'after a month', 'for the month', 'one each month', 'a month'; days → 'after {d} days', 'for the {d} days', 'one every {d} days', 'for each {d} days'.
(1) invalid: 'Fix the figure marked above to see the yearly rate.'
(2) nothing lent (one repayment, on the day): 'With one repayment made on the day, nothing is borrowed, so there is no rate to work out.'
(3) nothing reaches you: 'The fees and charges take all of the {amount}, so nothing reaches you and there is no rate to work out.' With first on the day: 'The fees and the first repayment take all of the {amount}, so nothing reaches you and there is no rate to work out.'
(4) repaid less (beyond rounding): 'The repayments add up to {repaid}, less than the {received} that reached you, so there is no cost to work out. Check each figure against the offer.'
(5) zero, exact: 'From these figures you pay back exactly what reached you: 0% a year. Anything not typed here, such as tax added to each instalment or a late fee, is not counted.'
(6) zero within rounding: 'From these figures you pay back what reached you, give or take {gap} of rounding in the instalments: 0% a year. Anything not typed here, such as tax added to each instalment or a late fee, is not counted.'
(7) rate, one repayment, first later: 'Getting {received} and repaying {repayment} {after} costs {cost}: {rate}% {forSpan}, which is {yearly} a year.' Default: 'Getting ₹5,000 and repaying ₹5,500 after 7 days costs ₹500: 10% for the 7 days, which is 521.4% a year.'
(8) rate, instalments, first later: 'Getting {received} and repaying {count} × {repayment}, {cadence}, costs {cost}: {rate}% {perUnit} on what is still owed, which is {yearly} a year.' The lesson's phone: 'Getting ₹11,400 and repaying 3 × ₹4,000, one each month, costs ₹600: 2.609% a month on what is still owed, which is 31.3% a year.'
(9) rate, first on the day: 'With {dayPaid} paid on the day, {received} is borrowed, and repaying {later} × {repayment}, {cadence}, costs {cost}: {rate}% {perUnit} on what is still owed, which is {yearly} a year.' (with later = 1: '…and repaying {repayment} {after} costs {cost}: {rate}% {forSpan}, which is {yearly} a year.') Phone paid on the day: 'With ₹4,600 paid on the day, ₹7,400 is borrowed, and repaying 2 × ₹4,000, one each month, costs ₹600: 5.359% a month on what is still owed, which is 64.3% a year.'
(10) very small: {yearly} = 'under 0.1%', e.g. 'Getting ₹1,00,000 and repaying ₹1,00,001 after a month costs ₹1: 0.001% for the month, which is under 0.1% a year.'
(11) very large: {rate} and/or {yearly} = 'over 10,000%', e.g. 'Getting ₹0.01 and repaying ₹5,500 after 7 days costs ₹5,499.99: over 10,000% for the 7 days, which is over 10,000% a year.'
No branch gives a verdict, compares offers or says the loan is fine.
revised.maths:
All pure, in src/lib/finance.ts. Shared helpers, exported for every new tool: toCents(x) = Math.round(x × 100) for money typed to the paisa; roundTo(x, dp) = Number(Math.round(Number(`${x}e${dp}`)) + `e-${dp}`), which avoids float slips (1.42251… → 1.423, 1.005 → 1.01).

yearlyRate(input: { amount: number | null; fee: number | null; repayment: number | null; count: number | null; period: 'week' | 'month' | 'days'; days: number | null; first: 'later' | 'on-the-day' }, basis: { monthsPerYear: number; daysPerYear: number } = { monthsPerYear: 12, daysPerYear: 365 }): YearlyRateResult, a union on kind.
1. Validate every field first; collect all errors; any error returns { kind: 'invalid', errors, notes } and no rate. amount: finite, > 0, ≤ 1e12. fee: null → 0; finite, ≥ 0, ≤ 1e12. repayment: finite, > 0, ≤ 1e12. count: n = Math.floor(count); finite and 1 ≤ n ≤ 600; a note 'count-floored' when n ≠ count. days (only when period = 'days'): d = Math.floor(days); finite and 1 ≤ d ≤ 3650; note 'days-floored' when d ≠ days.
2. later = first === 'on-the-day' ? n − 1 : n. later < 1 → { kind: 'nothing-lent' }.
3. Money in integer paise: amountC = toCents(amount), feeC = toCents(fee), repC = toCents(repayment), dayC = on-the-day ? repC : 0. receivedC = amountC − feeC − dayC; receivedC ≤ 0 → { kind: 'nothing-reaches-you', onTheDay }. repaidC = repC × later. gapC = repaidC − receivedC. tolerance = n paise (one per instalment typed: a lender may round each instalment up or down to the paisa).
4. periodsPerYear = period === 'month' ? basis.monthsPerYear : basis.daysPerYear / (period === 'week' ? 7 : d). No 28–31-day special case, so there is no jump between 29 and 30 days.
5. gapC < −n → { kind: 'repaid-less', received, repaid }. |gapC| ≤ n → { kind: 'zero', received, repaid, cost: 0, rounding: −gapC / 100, perPeriod: 0, yearlyShown: 0 }.
6. Otherwise solve for i, the rate per period on what reached you (received = receivedC/100, R = repC/100). later = 1: i = R / received − 1 exactly. later > 1: PV(i) = R × (1 − (1 + i)^−later) / i, strictly decreasing, PV(0⁺) = repaid > received. lo = 0, hi = 1; while PV(hi) > received and hi < 1e6, hi × 2. If PV(1e6) > received still: capped = true, i = 1e6 (display is 'over 10,000%' anyway); no loop can run past 20 doublings. Else 200 bisection steps (PV(mid) > received → lo = mid, else hi = mid), i = (lo + hi) / 2.
7. nominal = i × 100 × periodsPerYear (exact; tests and the 'within rounding' check). perPeriodDp = periodsPerYear ≤ 13 ? 3 : periodsPerYear ≤ 60 ? 4 : 5. perPeriodShown = roundTo(i × 100, perPeriodDp). yearlyShown = roundTo(perPeriodShown × periodsPerYear, 1): the headline is the rate shown times the periods in a year, so the ledger multiplies out exactly; it can differ from roundTo(nominal, 1) by one in the last place only near a .x5 boundary (rounding bound ≤ 0.0065 points monthly, ≤ 0.003 weekly, ≤ 0.0018 daily). compounded = ((1 + i)^periodsPerYear − 1) × 100, which may be Infinity. Returns { kind: 'rate', received, repaid, dayPaid: (feeC + dayC)/100, later, cost: gapC/100, periodsPerYear, perPeriod: i, perPeriodDp, perPeriodShown, yearlyShown, nominal, compounded, capped, notes }.

rateSchedule(result, repayment): only for kind 'rate', later > 1, not capped. In paise: owedC = receivedC; each row chargeC = Math.round(owedC × i), offC = repC − chargeC, owedC −= offC; the last row sets offC = owedC and paidC = owedC + chargeC, so it ends at exactly 0 and absorbs the rounding (must stay within ₹1 of the typed instalment). groupSchedule(rows, 12) when later > 60: rows '{from}–{to}' with summed paid, charge and paid off, and still owed at the group's end.

Display (src/lib/format.ts, ratePercent(value, locale, maxDp, floor)): not finite or > 10,000 → 'over 10,000%'; > 0 but rounds to 0 → 'under 0.1%' for the yearly figure, 'under 0.001%' (or the dp's step) for the period rate; else Intl.NumberFormat with minimumFractionDigits 0 and maximumFractionDigits maxDp, then '%'. Edge cases: blank fee is 0; negative, non-finite and out-of-range inputs never reach the solve; count and days not whole are rounded down with a note; zero cost within rounding shows a 'Rounding in the instalments' ledger row so the rows add up; very large rates never loop and never print a raw figure above 10,000%.

revised.howItWorks:
The rate is worked out on what reaches you: the amount borrowed minus the fees and charges taken at the start, and minus the first repayment if you said it is paid on the day. The cost of borrowing is everything you repay after that, minus what reached you.

One repayment: the rate for the period is the cost divided by what reached you. ₹500 on ₹5,000 is 10% for the 7 days.

Instalments: each one pays the period's charge on what is still owed, and the rest comes off. The tool finds the one rate per period at which your instalments pay off exactly what reached you; the table below shows it repayment by repayment. The first repayment is taken to fall one period after the money arrives, as on a Key Facts Statement's line for when repayments start, unless you chose 'on the day'. A lender's own schedule uses its interest rate on the full loan, so its rows differ from these.

The yearly rate is the rate for one period, as shown, times the periods in a year: 12 for a month, or 365 ÷ the days in each period (365 ÷ 7 for a week). Rates are rounded for display, and the yearly rate is worked out from the rate shown.

For equal monthly instalments with the fees taken at the start, this follows the method in the Reserve Bank's Key Facts Statement illustration: the rate at which the repayments are worth what reached you, times 12. There, ₹20,000 with ₹400 of fees and 24 instalments of ₹969.73 gives 17.07%; here it shows 17.1%. The statement's line calls this figure the "Effective annualized interest rate". If your result is not within rounding of the statement's APR, check for a charge you have not typed, a different first repayment date, unequal instalments, or GST you added that the statement's fee line leaves out.

For loans counted in days, a lender may turn the rate into a yearly one day by day, so its APR can differ from this. On the 7-day loan here, a daily rate times 365 gives 500.4% instead of 521.4%.

A flat rate is charged on the whole amount even as you repay it, so it is not a yearly rate: 18% flat on ₹20,000 over a year, 12 instalments of ₹1,966.67, works out to 31.7% a year here. Quick rules that roughly double a flat rate are only approximations; type the instalment printed on the offer.

If the same charge is paid period after period, it compounds to {compounded}% over a year. The headline does not use this figure.

Not counted: late fees, bounce charges and anything else charged only if something goes wrong, as an APR leaves them out; tax added to each instalment, unless you add it to the repayment; unequal instalments, a large last payment and months with no payment. For those, use the APR on the Key Facts Statement. A card's instalment plan has no Key Facts Statement; its charges are in the plan's terms and on the statement.

Nothing you type leaves this page. A copied link carries the numbers after the #, which browsers do not send to any server.

risks: Taken for the lender's APR: the result is labelled 'worked out from the figures above', the Key Facts Statement's APR is named as the figure a regulated lender prints, and How this is worked out lists why they can differ: an untyped charge, the first repayment date, unequal instalments, added GST, or a day-by-day APR on short loans.

The headline is computed from the rounded period rate so the ledger multiplies out exactly. Near a .x5 boundary it can differ from the unrounded rate by 0.1, and the footnote says so. The RBI pin shows 17.1% against the statement's 17.07%, and the page explains 'within rounding'.

Sensational figures: the headline and the period rate cap at 'over 10,000%'. The compounded figure sits only in the fold, framed as a charge 'paid period after period'. The default opens on 521.4% because that is the lesson's own figure.
Making a loan look acceptable: no branch judges the loan or compares offers, and the zero-cost sentence names what is not counted (tax on each instalment, late fees).

Double counting: a reader could add the first instalment to the fees and also choose 'on the day'. The fee hint does not mention instalments, and the First repayment control is the only route for them; content-reviewer should confirm the hints read clearly.

GST: the KFS may show fees net of GST, and the sources do not say whether its APR includes GST. The tool counts whatever the reader types and says the result can sit a little above the statement's figure if GST was added.

Whether the November 2025 consolidation folded the Digital Lending Directions into entity-wise directions could not be confirmed, because rbidocs.rbi.org.in returned a CAPTCHA. The tool's own copy relies only on the Responsible Business Conduct Directions (id=12942), but the lessons still cite 12848 for the cooling-off period and need a content-reviewer check. The Commercial Banks directions' KFS annex text (Annex XIII) was not read in full; its APR definition was.
The lesson edits (the 'effective rate' wording in details, the added sources) are the owner's call and go through content-reviewer. The `tool` lines are unchanged.
card-minimum dependency: cost-of-borrowing's moreTools gains card-minimum only when that tool ships for India. Until then the lessons test fails if it is added early.

India only: Europe's APRC is a compounded (effective) rate under Directive 2023/2225, and the US's Reg Z has its own convention. Neither is verified or taught by a lesson in those editions, so the method stays edition-bound and is passed as props.

revised.title: Take-home pay, line by line
revised.answers: How much of my pay actually reaches my account?
revised.intro: Answers one question: once every line on your payslip comes off, what reaches your account?

inputs.label: Where your payslip starts
options: ctc: Monthly CTC (from the offer letter)
gross: Gross salary (the payslip's own total)
inputs.hint: Most offers quote CTC; most payslips start at gross salary. Pick the figure you have in front of you.
inputs.source: example: in/money-basics/first-payslip starts at the ₹35,000 monthly CTC
inputs.validation: Whitelisted to 'ctc' or 'gross' whether it comes from the DOM or a link; anything else falls back to 'ctc'. Choosing 'gross' hides otherEmployerCosts and employerEpfPrinted and removes the employer's EPF line from the ledger.

inputs.label: First figure on the payslip. Set per edition and mode in regions.ts: India 'Monthly CTC' or 'Gross salary this month'; Europe 'Gross pay this month'; US 'Gross pay on this paycheck'
inputs.hint: India, CTC: 'CTC, cost to company: the yearly figure on the offer letter divided by 12. It counts money paid for you into funds, not only your pay.' India, gross: 'The payslip's own total of pay, before anything comes off.' Europe: 'The first money figure on your payslip, before anything comes off.' US: 'The gross pay line on your pay stub, for this paycheck only.'
inputs.source: example: the payslips in in/money-basics/first-payslip, eu/money-basics/first-payslip and us/money-basics/first-paycheck
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000. Blank or 0: no error text; the Figure shows '—' and the status line reads the no-start sentence. Negative: error text 'Type the amount without a minus sign.' under the field (aria-invalid), counted as 0. Above the max: 'That is more than this tool handles; check the figure.' When status is 'over', the field's aria-describedby also points at the status line (id thp-status).

inputs.label: Other parts of the CTC not paid to you each month
inputs.hint: Anything the offer counts in the CTC but does not pay you monthly: the employer's ESI (Employees' State Insurance) share, gratuity, insurance, admin charges, the monthly share of a yearly bonus. Copy it from the salary breakup; 0 if none.
inputs.source: Skeptic fix: CTC items other than the employer's EPF (Labour Law Reporter EPF page; glossary gratuity.json)
inputs.validation: Shown only when startFrom = 'ctc'. min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives 'Type the amount without a minus sign.' and counts as 0. Blank counts as 0. Its ledger line appears only when it is above 0, and it is subtracted before the 'Gross salary' subtotal.

inputs.label: How EPF is taken on this payslip
options: capped: 12% of PF wages up to the ₹25,000 ceiling (the ₹25,000 comes from the epfWageCeiling rule)
printed: As printed on my payslip
none: No EPF line on this payslip
inputs.hint: EPF, the Employees' Provident Fund. Pick what your payslip shows. Employers with fewer than 20 staff need not enrol you, a few notified employers use 10%, and above ₹25,000 of wages the extra is voluntary.
inputs.source: https://newsonair.gov.in/central-govt-notifies-employees-provident-fund-scheme-2026/ (12% of wages; 10% for notified establishments); https://newsonair.gov.in/cabinet-raises-epfo-mandatory-coverage-wage-ceiling-from-%E2%82%B915000-to-%E2%82%B925000/ ; https://labourlawreporter.com/epf.asp (20 or more employees)
inputs.validation: Whitelisted to all | capped | printed | none from DOM or link; anything else falls back to 'all'. 'all' and 'capped' show pfWages; 'printed' shows epfPrinted (and employerEpfPrinted when startFrom = 'ctc'); 'none' shows neither and drops both EPF lines.

inputs.label: PF wages a month: basic pay plus any dearness allowance (DA)
inputs.hint: From your salary breakup. Both EPF shares are 12% of this. If allowances such as HRA and special allowance are more than half your pay, the excess counts as wages too.
inputs.source: EPF Scheme 2026, 12% of wages (newsonair, 2 Jul 2026); Code on Social Security 2020 s.2(88) as summarised by Business Today, 11 Jul 2026: https://www.businesstoday.in/personal-finance/news/story/myth-busted-how-your-salary-has-changed-under-new-labour-codes-vs-epf-scheme-2026-542371-2026-07-11
inputs.validation: Shown when pfOn is 'all' or 'capped'. min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0. Blank or 0: a visible note 'No EPF worked out: PF wages are blank.' and both EPF lines are ₹0. Above the gross salary: note 'PF wages are part of your pay, so they are rarely above the gross salary; check the breakup.' (not blocking). Above ₹25,000 with pfOn 'all': the above-ceiling note. Below half of the gross salary: the half-of-pay note.

inputs.label: Your EPF line, as printed
inputs.hint: The EPF or PF line on your payslip, copied as it is.
inputs.source: Skeptic fix F2 (override when the computed share does not match the payslip)
inputs.validation: Shown only when pfOn = 'printed'. min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0. Blank: note 'Type your EPF line as printed.' and both EPF lines count as ₹0.

inputs.label: Employer's EPF share, from your salary breakup
inputs.hint: Leave it blank and the tool assumes it equals yours, and the ledger says so.
inputs.source: Skeptic fix F2
inputs.validation: Shown only when pfOn = 'printed' and startFrom = 'ctc'. Blank: employer share = your EPF line, ledger label 'Employer's EPF share, assumed equal to yours'. min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0.

inputs.label: Professional tax this month
inputs.hint: A state tax on jobs. Some states charge none, and the Constitution caps it at ₹2,500 a year. ₹200 is an example.
inputs.source: https://www.constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-276-taxes-on-professions-trades-callings-and-employments/
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0; blank counts as 0. Above ₹208 (floor of the ₹2,500 rule ÷ 12): note 'Professional tax is capped at ₹2,500 a year, about ₹208 a month; some states charge more in one month to reach the cap. Check the line against your payslip.' The typed amount is still used.

inputs.label: TDS this month, copied from your payslip
inputs.hint: TDS, tax deducted at source: income tax taken month by month. Copy it from your payslip; this tool never works it out. On the lesson's payslip it is ₹0.
inputs.source: https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/help/all-topics/e-filing-services/tds-compliance
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0; blank counts as 0. Its ₹0 line stays in the ledger (it is a payslip line) but is not counted in lineCount.

inputs.label: Other lines on your payslip (India) / Other lines on the stub (US): a list of rows, each a name and an amount
inputs.hint: India: 'ESI (Employees' State Insurance) appears at lower pay; a labour welfare fund, or any other line. Copy each as printed.' US: 'State disability or paid-leave insurance, city or local tax, a health plan, retirement: copy each as printed.'
inputs.source: Skeptic fixes S1-3, S1-5 and F1. No ESI rate is printed: it could not be confirmed on esic.gov.in on 22 Sep 2026 (connection refused).
inputs.validation: 0 to 5 rows, added with 'Add a line' (disabled at 5, with the text 'Up to 5 lines; add the rest together into one.') and removed per row. Name: text input, maxlength 40, blank name shown as 'Other line {n}'. Amount: as a money field, min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error under that row and counts as 0. Link key 'others', encoded 'name~amount|name~amount' by src/lib/lines-link.ts (max 5 rows on decode, name cut to 40, amount cut to 16 characters and parsed; unreadable amounts become 0).

inputs.label: The lines on your payslip, each with the name your payslip gives it
inputs.hint: Name each line as your payslip does, for example long-term care insurance, church tax, PRSI or USC. Countries print different lines. The four here are the lesson's example.
inputs.source: example (eu/money-basics/first-payslip); https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/moving-working-europe/eu-social-security-coordination_en
inputs.validation: 1 to 8 rows, prefilled with the lesson's four. 'Add a line' disabled at 8 ('Up to 8 lines; add the rest together into one.'). Name maxlength 40, blank shown as 'Line {n}'. Amount min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives 'Type the amount without a minus sign. A line that adds money back is not handled here.' and counts as 0. Each row prints 'comes to {x.x}% of gross' when gross is above 0. Link key 'lines', same codec, max 8 rows.

inputs.label: Employer contributions, if your payslip prints them
inputs.hint: Paid by the employer on top of gross pay. Shown beside the answer, never taken off your pay. Leave it blank if your payslip does not print it.
inputs.source: example (eu/money-basics/first-payslip)
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0. Blank or 0: the employer facts are hidden, not shown as €0.

inputs.label: Regular hours on this paycheck
inputs.hint: The regular hours this paycheck pays for. Check them against your own note of the shifts you worked.
inputs.source: example (us/money-basics/first-paycheck)
inputs.validation: min 0, max 744 ('More hours than a month holds; check the stub.'); negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0. Blank or 0 hides the hours check; the gross line drives the sum either way.

inputs.label: Hourly rate
inputs.hint: The rate in your offer.
inputs.source: example (us/money-basics/first-paycheck)
inputs.validation: min 0, max 10,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0. Blank or 0 hides the hours check.

inputs.label: Overtime hours on this paycheck
inputs.hint: Hours over 40 in a week, paid at least 1.5 times the rate under federal law. 0 if none.
inputs.source: https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime
inputs.validation: min 0, max 744; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0; blank counts as 0.

inputs.label: Social Security, as on your stub
inputs.hint: Part of FICA, the Social Security and Medicare taxes. Copy it from your stub; the tool checks it against 6.2% of gross.
inputs.source: https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751 ; exceptions: https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/student-exception-to-fica-tax , https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/family-employees , https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/foreign-student-liability-for-social-security-and-medicare-taxes , https://www.irs.gov/government-entities/federal-state-local-governments/faqs-for-government-entities-regarding-cafeteria-plans
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0; blank counts as 0. Never overwritten by the computed 6.2%.

inputs.label: Medicare, as on your stub
inputs.hint: The other FICA line. Copy it from your stub; the tool checks it against 1.45% of gross.
inputs.source: https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751
inputs.validation: As socialSecurity.

inputs.label: Federal income tax withheld, copied from your stub
inputs.hint: Set by your W-4, the withholding form you filled in when you started. The tool never works it out. $110 is this stub's figure.
inputs.source: https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-w-4
inputs.validation: min 0, max 1,000,000,000; negative gives the minus-sign error and counts as 0; blank counts as 0 (an exempt W-4 is typed as 0).

inputs.label: State income tax withheld, copied from your stub
inputs.hint: Depends on your state, and some states have none: type 0 then.
inputs.source: https://www.usa.gov/state-taxes
inputs.validation: As federal.

inputs.label: How often you are paid
inputs.hint: Every two weeks is 26 paychecks in most years and 27 in some.
inputs.source: calendar arithmetic (PAYDAYS in finance.ts), not a rule
inputs.validation: Whitelisted by parsePayFrequency from DOM or link; any other value (for example 'daily') falls back to 'fortnightly', so n is never undefined.

rules.label: EPF: 12% of wages each from you and from your employer (EPF Scheme 2026, in force from 29 June 2026)
rules.sourceTitle: Central govt notifies Employees' Provident Fund Scheme 2026 (Akashvani News, 2 July 2026)

rules.label: A few establishments notified by the central government keep a 10% rate (used in hint and How this is worked out text only; the tool never computes it, 'As printed' covers it)
rules.sourceTitle: Central govt notifies Employees' Provident Fund Scheme 2026 (Akashvani News, 2 July 2026)

rules.label: Wage ceiling for compulsory EPF, a month, from 17 September 2026 (was ₹15,000)
rules.sourceTitle: Cabinet raises EPFO mandatory coverage wage ceiling from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 (Akashvani News, 17 September 2026)

rules.label: Where contributions are held to the ceiling, 12% of ₹25,000 is ₹3,000 a side (was ₹1,800); above it the contribution is voluntary
rules.sourceTitle: Raising the EPFO bar: central government increases wage ceiling to INR 25,000 (National Law Review, 21 September 2026)

rules.label: Basic pay, DA and retaining allowance must be at least 50% of total remuneration; allowances beyond half count as wages for PF (Code on Social Security 2020, in force 21 November 2025). Secondary source; confirm on labour.gov.in before shipping
rules.sourceTitle: Myth busted: how your salary has changed under new labour codes vs EPF Scheme 2026 (Business Today, 11 July 2026)

rules.label: EPF applies to establishments with 20 or more employees. Secondary source; confirm on epfindia.gov.in before shipping
rules.sourceTitle: EPF under the Code on Social Security (Labour Law Reporter, accessed 22 September 2026)

rules.label: Professional tax on one person may not exceed ₹2,500 a year (Article 276(2))
rules.sourceTitle: Article 276, Constitution of India (Centre for Law and Policy Research)

rules.label: Social Security: 6.2% of wages from you, the same again from the employer (used only in the check row)
rules.sourceTitle: Topic no. 751, Social Security and Medicare withholding rates (IRS, updated 20 January 2026)

rules.label: Medicare: 1.45% of wages from you, the same again from the employer (used only in the check row)

rules.label: Wages in a year above which the extra 0.9% Medicare is withheld
rules.sourceTitle: Topic no. 751, Social Security and Medicare withholding rates (IRS, updated 20 January 2026)

rules.label: Overtime is paid at not less than 1.5 times the regular rate
rules.sourceTitle: Overtime pay (US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division; page undated, accessed 22 September 2026)

rules.label: Overtime applies to hours over 40 in a workweek
rules.sourceTitle: Overtime pay (US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division; page undated, accessed 22 September 2026)

outputs: Headline (Figure), shown only when status is 'ok', otherwise '—': India ₹30,600 'In-hand pay a month'; Europe €1,150 'Net pay this month'; US $1,317.60 'Net pay on this paycheck'.

Ledger, India, CTC start (default): Monthly CTC ₹35,000; − Employer's EPF share (12% of ₹17,500 PF wages) ₹2,100; [− Other parts of the CTC, only when above 0]; = Gross salary ₹32,900; − Your EPF share (12% of ₹17,500 PF wages) ₹2,100; − Professional tax ₹200; − TDS (copied from your payslip) ₹0; − each 'other' row by its own name; double-ruled In-hand pay ₹30,600. Label variants: '(12% of PF wages up to ₹25,000)' when capped and PF wages are above ₹25,000; '(as printed)' for 'printed'; 'Employer's EPF share, assumed equal to yours' when the employer field is blank; both EPF lines absent for 'none'. Gross start: Gross salary ₹32,900; − Your EPF share ₹2,100; − Professional tax ₹200; − TDS ₹0; double-ruled In-hand pay ₹30,600, with no employer line.

Ledger, Europe: Gross pay €1,500; − Pension contribution €135, comes to 9.0% of gross; − Health cover €135, 9.0%; − Unemployment cover €30, 2.0%; − Income tax €50, 3.3%; double-ruled Net pay €1,150. The names are the reader's own row names.

Ledger, US (all money with two decimals): Gross pay $1,600.00; − Social Security $99.20; − Medicare $23.20; − Federal income tax $110.00; − State income tax $50.00; − each 'other' row by name; double-ruled Net pay $1,317.60.

Checks list under the US ledger (a <ul>, text only, never the word 'error'): 'Hours: 80 at $20.00 is $1,600.00, the same as the gross line.' (with overtime: '80 at $20.00, plus 4 overtime hours at $30.00, is $1,720.00, the same as the gross line.'; mismatch beyond 1 cent: 'Hours: 80 at $20.00 is $1,600.00; the gross line is $1,650.00, $50.00 more. Overtime, tips, a second rate or a bonus can explain a difference. If none applies, ask payroll, with your shift notes and your offer.'; hidden when hours or rate is 0). 'Social Security: 6.2% of $1,600.00 is $99.20, the same as the stub.' / on a difference beyond 1 cent: 'Social Security: 6.2% of $1,600.00 is $99.20; the stub shows $0.00. A pre-tax health plan lowers the pay this is worked on; students working for their own school, under-18s working in a business owned only by a parent, and some international students on F-1 or J-1 student visas pay none. Payroll can say which applies.' Medicare the same with 1.45%.

Facts, India: CTC start 'Into the provident fund and pension scheme for you, both shares' ₹4,200; gross start 'Your EPF share, kept in a fund in your name' ₹2,100 plus the words 'Your employer adds its own share outside this sum.'; hidden when EPF is 0. Europe (hidden when employer contributions are blank or 0): 'Your employer pays on top' €300 and 'What the job costs your employer' €1,800. US: 'Your employer pays the same Social Security and Medicare again' $122.40 (hidden when both typed lines are 0); 'A year, if every paycheck matched this one' $34,257.60; 'A usual month, if every paycheck matched this one: two paychecks' $2,635.20.

Notes (plain text under the ledger, each only when triggered): India half-of-pay note, above-ceiling note, PF-wages-blank note, printed-blank note, PF-wages-above-pay note, professional-tax-above-₹208 note; US wage-base note when gross × paychecks a year passes $184,500 ('At this pay, a year's wages would pass $184,500, where Social Security stops (IRS Topic 751), so later stubs in the year may show none.') with ', and above $200,000 an extra 0.9% of Medicare is withheld' appended when gross × paychecks passes $200,000.

Rules as of line (server-rendered RulesLine.astro under the tool, India and US only): 'Rules as of 22 September 2026:' then each rule's label with its source link and date: India EPF 12% of wages (EPF Scheme 2026), the ₹25,000 wage ceiling from 17 Sep 2026 and ₹3,000 a side at it, professional tax cap ₹2,500 a year; US Social Security 6.2%, Medicare 1.45%, the $184,500 wage base, the 0.9% over $200,000 (IRS Topic 751), overtime at 1.5 times over 40 hours (DOL). Europe has no rules line: nothing in the Europe tool depends on a rate.

Budget hand-off link under the result, hidden unless status is 'ok': 'Plan the month in the budget planner' to {prefix}/tools/budget#income={net} (India, Europe) or #income={usualMonth} with the words ', starting from two paychecks, if each matched this one' (US; 'four' weekly, 'two' twice a month, 'one' monthly). The figure goes after the #, never in the query.

Terms on this page (server-rendered in [tool].astro, links to {base}/glossary#{id}): India ctc, gross-pay, basic-pay, epf, eps, wage-ceiling, professional-tax, tds, esi (new), gratuity, in-hand-pay; Europe payslip, gross-pay, net-pay, social-contributions, employer-contributions; US pay-stub, gross-pay, fica, w-4, withholding, net-pay, hourly-rate.

Copy link and Share (ToolActions) write the inputs after the # only, with the line 'The link carries the numbers on screen after the #, which browsers do not send to any server. Anyone you send it to sees them.'
revised.resultSentence:
One status line (p.plain, id thp-status). {ofStart} is per mode: India CTC 'Of a monthly CTC of {start}'; India gross 'Of a gross salary of {start}'; Europe 'Of gross pay of {start} this month'; US 'Of gross pay of {start} on this paycheck'. {startNoun} is 'monthly CTC' | 'gross salary' | 'gross pay'. {lineCountWords} is one to ten in words, digits above ten, and 'line' or 'lines' agrees.
(1) status 'no-start' (start blank, 0 or negative): 'Type the top figure on your payslip, the {startNoun}, to see what reaches your account.'
(2) status 'over', net below 0: 'These lines add up to {deducted}, more than the {startNoun} of {start}. Check each one against your payslip; the answer is held back until they fit.' The Figure shows '—' and every fact, the yearly projection and the budget link are hidden.
(3) status 'over', net exactly 0: 'These lines add up to the whole {startNoun} of {start}, so nothing would reach your account. Check each one against your payslip.' Same things hidden.
(4) status 'ok', lineCount 0: '{ofStart}, all of it reaches your account, because every line is 0. Check that against your payslip.'
(5) status 'ok', otherwise: '{ofStart}, {net} reaches your account: {netShare}% of it. {deducted} comes off in {lineCountWords} {line|lines}' followed by exactly one ending:
  India, CTC start, EPF above 0: ', and {fundTotal} of that goes into the provident fund and pension scheme for you.'
  India, gross start, EPF above 0: ', and {yours} of that is your own EPF share, kept in a fund in your name. Your employer adds its own share outside this sum.'
  India with no EPF, and Europe: '.'
  US fortnightly: '. If every paycheck matched this one, {n} paychecks make {year} a year; most months hold two, {usualMonth}, and usually two months a year hold a third.'
  US weekly: '. If every paycheck matched this one, {n} paychecks make {year} a year; most months hold four, {usualMonth}, and usually four months a year hold a fifth.'
  US twice a month: '. If every paycheck matched this one, {n} paychecks make {year} a year, two in every month, {usualMonth}.'
  US monthly: '. If every paycheck matched this one, {n} paychecks make {year} a year, one each month.'
Europe adds, only when employer contributions are above 0, a second sentence: 'Your employer pays {employerOnTop} on top, so the job costs it {employerCost}.'
Examples at the defaults. India: 'Of a monthly CTC of ₹35,000, ₹30,600 reaches your account: 87.4% of it. ₹4,400 comes off in three lines, and ₹4,200 of that goes into the provident fund and pension scheme for you.' Europe: 'Of gross pay of €1,500 this month, €1,150 reaches your account: 76.7% of it. €350 comes off in four lines. Your employer pays €300 on top, so the job costs it €1,800.' US: 'Of gross pay of $1,600.00 on this paycheck, $1,317.60 reaches your account: 82.4% of it. $282.40 comes off in four lines. If every paycheck matched this one, 26 paychecks make $34,257.60 a year; most months hold two, $2,635.20, and usually two months a year hold a third.'
revised.maths:
All in src/lib/finance.ts (pure, no DOM), money in integer cents.
Shared helpers, exported: toCents(v) = 0 when v is not finite, else sign(v) × Math.round(Number((|v| × 100).toPrecision(12))), which rounds half away from zero on the decimal as typed (575.625 → 57563, 1.005 → 101) where a bare Math.round(v × 100) slips a cent. fromCents(c) = c / 100. roundMoney(v) = fromCents(toCents(v)). shareOf(cents, ratePercent) = Math.round(cents × Math.round(ratePercent × 100) / 10000): integer numerator, basis points, half-up; this fixes the float slips the skeptic found ($150 Medicare 2.18 not 2.17; $162.50 Social Security 10.08 not 10.07). percent1(partCents, wholeCents) = wholeCents > 0 ? Math.round(partCents × 1000 / wholeCents) / 10 : null (an integer division is correctly rounded, so 823.5 stays 823.5 and rounds to 82.4). deductions(start, lines) is rewritten on cents (running = start cents minus each line's cents); every existing pin is unchanged. line(v) = finite and above 0 ? v : 0: negatives are flagged by the island and count as 0 here too.
PAYDAYS = { weekly: 52, fortnightly: 26, 'twice-monthly': 24, monthly: 12 }; parsePayFrequency(value, fallback) returns value when it is a key of PAYDAYS, else fallback.
perMonth(perPay, n) = { year: fromCents(toCents(perPay) × n), usualCount: floor(n / 12), usualMonth: fromCents(toCents(perPay) × floor(n / 12)), monthsWithExtra: n − 12 × floor(n / 12) }.
takeHome(input) with input a union on mode. Common result: { lines: { label, amount, subtotalLabel?, kind }[], running, net, deducted, lineCount (lines whose cents are above 0), status, netShare }. status = 'no-start' when start cents ≤ 0; else 'over' when net cents ≤ 0; else 'ok'. netShare = percent1(net cents, start cents) only when status is 'ok', else null.
Mode 'epf' (India), input { startFrom: 'ctc'|'gross', start, otherEmployerCosts, pfOn: 'all'|'capped'|'printed'|'none', pfWages, epfPrinted: number|null, employerEpfPrinted: number|null, professionalTax, tds, others: {label, amount}[], rules: { epfRate, epfWageCeiling, professionalTaxYearCap } } (rules come from the page's edition). EPF: 'all' → yours = employer = Math.round(toCents(line(pfWages)) × Math.round(epfRate × 100) / 1,000,000), which is whole rupees (EPFO rounds to the rupee, so ₹17,504 gives ₹2,100, not ₹2,100.48; an integer PF wage can never land on half a rupee because 12 × wages ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 hundredths). 'capped' → the same on min(line(pfWages), epfWageCeiling). 'printed' → yours = line(epfPrinted); employer = employerEpfPrinted is null ? yours (employerAssumed = true) : line(employerEpfPrinted). 'none' → both 0. Lines in order: when startFrom = 'ctc', employer's EPF share (if above 0) then 'Other parts of the CTC' (if above 0), the last of these carrying subtotalLabel 'Gross salary'. Then 'Your EPF share' (omitted when pfOn = 'none'), 'Professional tax', 'TDS', then each others row (max 5). gross = the running figure after the CTC-only lines, or start. Notes: halfRule = pfOn is 'all' or 'capped' and pfWages > 0 and 2 × pfWages cents < gross cents; aboveCeiling = pfOn = 'all' and pfWages > epfWageCeiling; wagesBlank = pfOn is 'all' or 'capped' and pfWages ≤ 0; printedBlank = pfOn = 'printed' and epfPrinted is null or 0; pfWagesAbovePay = pfWages > gross; ptAboveMonthly = professionalTax > floor(professionalTaxYearCap / 12) (208). fundTotal = startFrom 'ctc' ? yours + employer : yours; null when 0. The pension/fund split of the employer's share is never computed (EPS runs on a ₹15,000 pension ceiling the sources here do not confirm after 17 Sep 2026).
Mode 'typed' (Europe), input { start, rows: {label, amount}[] (1–8), employerOnTop: number|null }: lines = the rows in order. impliedPercents[i] = percent1(row cents, start cents) (null when start ≤ 0). employerCost = line(employerOnTop) > 0 and start > 0 ? fromCents(start cents + employerOnTop cents) : null; it is a fact outside the chain, never subtracted.
Mode 'fica' (US), input { start, hours, hourlyRate, overtimeHours, socialSecurity, medicare, federal, state, others (max 5), paidEvery, rules: { socialSecurityRate, medicareRate, socialSecurityWageBase, additionalMedicareThreshold, overtimeMultiplier } }: lines = [Social Security, Medicare, Federal income tax, State income tax, ...others], every amount as typed; the stub's gross, never hours × rate, drives the sum. checks.socialSecurity = { expected: fromCents(shareOf(start cents, 6.2)), diff: fromCents(typed cents − expected cents), match: |diff cents| ≤ 1 }; checks.medicare the same with 1.45. checks.hours = line(hours) > 0 and line(hourlyRate) > 0 ? { expected: fromCents(toCents(hours × rate + overtimeHours × rate × 1.5)), diff: fromCents(start cents − expected cents), match: |diff cents| ≤ 1 } : null (the 1-cent tolerance absorbs payroll's sub-cent rounding: 37.5 × $15.35 = $575.625 printed as $575.62). employerMatch = typed Social Security + Medicare cents when above 0, else null (typed, not computed: it follows the wage base the stub actually used). n = PAYDAYS[parsePayFrequency(paidEvery, 'fortnightly')]. wageBaseNote = start cents × n > socialSecurityWageBase × 100; additionalMedicareNote = start cents × n > additionalMedicareThreshold × 100. projection = perMonth(net, n) only when status is 'ok'.
Display (island): money uses the edition's locale only. twoDecimals = mode 'fica' or any start, line, running figure, net or fact with cents; then money(v, locale, 2) for every ledger row, the Figure and the facts, else money(v, locale, 0). Percentages are number(p, locale, 1) + '%' from the already-rounded value, never percent(net / start) (which prints 82.3% for the US default). Values are never recomputed in the island; it formats what takeHome returns.

revised.howItWorks: India: The tool takes each line off in the order a payslip prints it. It works out one thing only: the two provident fund shares, each 12% of your PF wages, in whole rupees. It can also work them out on wages up to the ₹25,000 ceiling, where the compulsory share stops at ₹3,000 a side, or take the amount printed on your payslip. PF wages are basic pay plus any dearness allowance. Under the labour codes, allowances above half your pay count as wages too. This tool does not work that out, so if your EPF line differs, pick 'As printed'. A few notified employers use 10%, and employers with fewer than 20 staff need not enrol you. Part of the employer's share goes to the pension scheme rather than to your fund; the tool does not split it. Professional tax, TDS, ESI and every other line are copied from your payslip. The tool never works out income tax or the tax regime. Professional tax cannot pass ₹2,500 a year. The ₹35,000 payslip is the lesson's example. Europe: Every line is copied from your payslip, under the name your payslip gives it, and taken off gross pay in order. Beside each line the tool prints the share of gross pay it comes to, so you can see your own country's rates. It knows no country's rates, and it never works out tax or contributions. Employer contributions are paid on top of gross pay: they are shown beside the answer and never taken off your pay. A refund, or any line that adds money back, is not handled; add it to net pay yourself. The €1,500 payslip and its 9%, 9%, 2% and €50 lines are the lesson's example, not any country's rules. United States: The tool takes each line on the stub off gross pay, in order, as printed, and works out nothing the stub already says. It checks two things. First, that regular hours times the rate, plus overtime at 1.5 times the rate, match the gross line. Federal law pays overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek. Tips, a shift premium, a second rate or a bonus also change gross, so a difference is a question for payroll, not a verdict. Second, that Social Security is 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% of gross. Both can rightly differ. A pre-tax health plan lowers the pay they are worked on. Students working for their own school pay neither, nor do under-18s working in a business owned only by a parent, nor some international students on F-1 or J-1 student visas in their first five years. Social Security stops once a year's wages pass $184,500 in 2026; Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% applies to wages over $200,000 in a year (IRS Topic 751). Federal and state income tax, and every other line, are copied from the stub. The tool never works out withholding, and does not recompute it for a 401(k) or a health plan. The yearly and monthly figures assume every paycheck matches this one. Every two weeks gives 26 paychecks in most years and 27 in some; weekly gives 52, sometimes 53. Money is counted in whole cents, rounded half up, as payroll does. All editions: nothing you type leaves your browser. A copied link carries the numbers after the #, which browsers do not send to any server.

changes: S1-1 (facts: EPF is 12% of wages, not of basic): taken. basicPercent is replaced by an amount, pfWages ('PF wages a month: basic pay plus any dearness allowance'), default 17,500, with the skeptic's hint about allowances above half of pay. The ledger label reads '(12% of ₹17,500 PF wages)' and the rule reads 'EPF 12% of wages (EPF Scheme 2026, from 29 June 2026)', re-checked on newsonair on 22 Sep 2026. The half-of-pay note fires when PF wages are under half of gross salary. The add-back itself is not computed: the sources disagree on what 'total remuneration' is (Business Today says total remuneration, Labour Law Reporter says CTC), so the note says 'may be higher' and sends the reader to 'As printed'.

S1-2 (the ₹25,000 ceiling): taken, as the pfOn select with 'all' / 'capped' / 'none'. The pin pfWages 30,000 capped gives ₹3,000. The note is reworded from 'many employers cap it' to 'an employer may cap both shares there': no source opened gives a proportion, and Business Today confirms only that employers can cap and need not match voluntary contributions. The '20 staff' hint is kept, citing Labour Law Reporter (secondary: the PIB and EPFO pages returned 403 or refused the connection).

S1-3 and F1 (missing lines): both taken, in one form. India gets otherEmployerCosts (CTC-only parts, before the Gross salary subtotal) as skeptic 1 specified. Skeptic 1's single otherDeductions field became skeptic 2's labelled 'Other lines' rows (up to 5), so each printed line keeps its own name in the ledger. The ESI rate and ceiling (F1 wanted '0.75% when gross is ₹21,000 or less' in the hint) are NOT printed: esic.gov.in refused the connection on 22 Sep 2026 and PIB returned 403. Skeptic 1's condition (confirm on esic.gov.in, then enter it as a Rule) is not met, so the hint says only that an ESI line appears at lower pay. Copying it as printed keeps the answer right.

S1-4 and F3 (US FICA always computed): taken. Social Security and Medicare are typed as printed and prefilled with $99.20 and $23.20; 6.2% and 1.45% are used only in the check rows, and the check wording lists the student, parent's-business and F-1/J-1 exceptions and Section 125 plans (all four IRS pages opened 22 Sep 2026). Conflict on employerMatch: F3 said use the computed amounts, S1 said use the typed ones. I took the typed ones. The employer pays on the same FICA wages the stub used, so a computed 7.65% of gross would overstate the match under a pre-tax health plan and invent one for an exempt student. It is hidden when both typed lines are 0, as F3 asked. F3's wage-base and $200,000 notes are taken, both measured on a year (gross × paychecks), because a single paycheck over $200,000 never happens for this audience.

S1-5 (US other deductions): taken as labelled rows, not a single field (see F1). The edge case is reworded: pre-tax 401(k) and health lines are typed in 'Other lines', FICA is copied from the stub, and the tool never recomputes a lowered wage base.

S1-6 (Europe's four fixed labels): taken. There are reader-labelled rows (up to 8), prefilled with the lesson's four and each printing 'comes to x.x% of gross', with the skeptic's hint. The risks wording becomes 'the reader copies each printed line, so any country's payslip can be entered'. TK 2026 is not cited because the hint names no rate.

S1-8 and F6 (payday count): taken. The ending has four forms (every month holds two for twice a month; one each month for monthly; 'usually two months a year hold a third' for every two weeks; 'usually four … a fifth' for weekly). F11 (mixed decimals): taken. Two decimals are used everywhere in US mode, or whenever any figure has cents; otherwise none. e2e asserts '$1,600.00' and '$110.00'.

F13 (the lessons link to no tool): the goal is taken and the mechanism changed. F13's default `d.tool ?? 'take-home-pay'` on DeductionExplorer is wrong: 14 lessons use deduction explorables (for example bnpl, platform-fees, both income statements, first-cushion, moving-out, pricing-abroad, profit-vs-cash, side-income-tax), and several have no tool or a different one. Instead, LessonLayout renders a server-side link for each slug in [tool, ...moreTools] after any deduction or drill explorable, as the registry's LessonLayout change already specifies. It works with JavaScript off. The budget planner keeps the three lessons through moreTools: [budget] and the related filter.

F15 (a test that fails on a date): taken. The freshness check moves to scripts/rules-freshness.mjs (warn at 11 months, fail at 12, plus reviewBy), run by ship-check. The unit test checks shape only. This replaces the registry's 'asOf within 12 months' Vitest assertion, and the scheduled CI job is left to Rajvir because workflows are protected files.

F16 (undefined jargon): taken. Every hint that meets an acronym starts with or contains its expansion (CTC, EPF, TDS, ESI, DA, FICA, W-4). A 'Terms on this page' list links the edition's glossary entries, a new esi.json entry has no rate, and a unit test checks both.

Other changes. minutes goes from 2 to 3, for the extra controls. The US hours label becomes 'Regular hours', so overtime is not counted twice. The start label comes per mode from regions.ts. The Rules line now carries the ceiling's ₹3,000 effect, the professional tax cap, the wage base and overtime. Europe gets no Rules line, because nothing there depends on a rate.
risks: The India rules rest partly on secondary sources. The 50% wages rule is from Business Today and Labour Law Reporter, the 20-employee coverage from Labour Law Reporter, and the ₹3,000 cap at the ceiling from National Law Review. Official pages (PIB, epfindia.gov.in, esic.gov.in, the gazette) returned 403 or refused the connection on 22 Sep 2026. The content-reviewer should confirm each on an official page before shipping and swap the source URLs; the tool's arithmetic does not change.

ESI is not modelled. The reader copies it as printed, and no rate or ceiling appears until confirmed on esic.gov.in and entered as a Rule. A reader who does not notice the ESI line on the payslip gets an in-hand figure that is too high. The hint names ESI to lower that risk.

The wording differs between lesson and tool. The India lesson body and takeaway, and glossary basic-pay.json and epf.json, say EPF is 12% of basic pay, while the tool says 12% of PF wages (basic plus DA, with allowances above half of pay added). It is correct for the lesson's example: allowances of ₹15,400 are under half of the ₹32,900 gross. The content-reviewer should decide whether to align that prose. It is not changed here, because the lesson files carry uncommitted edits on this branch.

The India inputs are long: up to nine controls plus rows. Selects reveal only the fields in use, and fieldsets ('Where your payslip starts', 'Provident fund', 'Taxes and other lines') group them. Check the 360px screenshot to see that the result is reachable without heavy scrolling, and that the design-reviewer accepts the density.

Advice risk stays low but needs review. No line computes income tax, TDS, withholding or a tax regime. The only computed amounts are the EPF shares (overridable) and the check rows, which never say 'error' and always send the reader to payroll or the payslip. The content-reviewer should read every check and note string.

The yearly and monthly figures are projections. They are labelled 'if every paycheck matched this one', which a reader with changing shifts could still read as a promise. The budget link carries the same words.

Rules go stale: the US wage base changes each January (reviewBy 2027-01-15), and India's labour-code rules are still being notified (reviewBy 2027-03-22). The freshness script only warns if ship-check is run; without the scheduled job, which is Rajvir's decision, nothing flags them on a quiet branch.

The # fragment is removed after load, so a reload shows the typed or default figures, not the shared ones. A copied link still reveals the figures to whoever receives it, which the line beside the button says. The budget navigation adds one history entry whose fragment is then replaced. Browsers differ on whether the global history keeps the original URL, so on a shared phone the figures may still appear in history.
Refunds and lines that add pay (for example an Irish PAYE refund) are not supported. Such payslips need a manual step, which How this is worked out says.
The JS budget: the new island plus the codec is expected at about 5–6 KB gzipped on a page well under 90 KB. js-budget.mjs must confirm it.
The kit's hash-first link reading and fragment clearing touch every calculator. Keep the existing ?-link e2e tests green before merging.

revised.maths:
No money arithmetic. The pure functions live in src/lib/drills.ts, a new file with no DOM, unit-tested, and in src/lib/progress.ts.

numberWord(n): 'One' to 'Ten' for integers 1 to 10. It throws for anything else, so a merged set over 10 fails the build.

drillIntro(total, ordinary, scope?): `${numberWord(total)} screens${scope ? ' ' + scope : ''}. ${numberWord(ordinary)} ${ordinary === 1 ? 'is an ordinary payment' : 'are ordinary payments'}, so refusing everything is not the answer.` Examples: (6,2) gives 'Six screens. Two are ordinary payments, so refusing everything is not the answer.' (6,2,'on the way to paying') gives the Europe line.

drillSet(lesson, bank, region): (1) The lesson's explorable.scenarios in lesson order, with checkId `${lesson.id}#d${i+1}`. These are the ids the lesson already writes, so one screen is never two review items. (2) The bank's scenarios in file order, with checkId `${region}/tools/${bank.tool}#${s.id}`. It returns { scenarios, total, ordinary: the count of s.ordinary === true, intro: drillIntro(total, ordinary, bank.scope) }. There is no shuffle and no tally.

reviewContext(screen, localeCode): [`${from}:`, amount === undefined ? '' : money(amount, localeByCode(localeCode)), ...lines, action ? `[${action}]` : ''] with empty parts filtered out, joined by one space. checks.json.ts uses it for lesson drill scenarios and bank scenarios alike, so the amount now reaches review. That fixes 'check the amount' being impossible at review time.

screenHosts(text): every match of /\b(?:[a-z0-9-]+\.)+[a-z]{2,}\b(?:\/[^\s]*)?/gi, mapped to new URL('https://' + token).hostname. A screen passes when every host ends in '.example'. The last label must be letters, so '₹1.00' is never read as a host.

isQuizCheck(id) = /#q\d+$/.test(id). It replaces includes('#q') in LessonScript.

schedule(progress, id, correct, now), new rule in src/lib/progress.ts: let item = progress.review?.[id] and today = dayString(now). If correct && item && item.due.slice(0,10) > today, return progress unchanged (same object): no promotion before the item is due. Otherwise the rule is as before: box = correct ? min(5, (item?.box ?? 0) + 1) : 1, and due = today + BOX_DAYS[box]. A wrong answer always resets to box 1, due tomorrow.

nextReturnFor(progress, ids): the earliest review.due among the given ids, as a local-midnight Date via dayToDate, or null when none is scheduled. It is used because the tool's ids share no single prefix.

titleFor(tool, region) = tool.titles?.[region] ?? tool.title.

RegionTabs edition href: `${base}/${code}` + (sub ? '/' + (subRegions && !subRegions.includes(code) ? sub.split('/')[0] : sub) : '').

Edge cases:
- Bank missing: no page and no index row.
- fromLesson missing, in another edition, or not a drill: drills.test.ts fails and the page is skipped.
- Duplicate bank ids: the schema refine fails the build, and checks.json.ts also throws on a duplicate key.
- A non-integer amount fails the schema (amount is int).
- ordinary < 2, ordinary > total − 2 or ordinary × 3 < total: the test fails.
- A reveal with no pick: box 1, due tomorrow, and the status says so.
- The lesson and the tool on the same day: the second correct answer leaves box 1, due tomorrow.
- JS off: nothing is scored and the return line stays hidden.
- storage undefined: saveProgress(undefined, …) returns true today, so the line is filled only when storage !== undefined && saveProgress(...) === true.

revised.howItWorks:
There are no sums here. The six screens are made up and drawn on the page, and none of them names a real bank, app, company or regulator. The first come from the lesson behind this drill, and the rest are this drill's own. Each reveal names the behaviour that gives a scam away, or the one that shows a payment is ordinary. Two of the six are ordinary, because refusing every payment is not safety. The sources under the set back each cue.

On this device, each situation you reveal joins your review. A right answer comes back after a day, then after longer gaps. A wrong answer, or a reveal with no pick, comes back tomorrow. Answering again before a situation is due changes nothing. Your picks stay in this browser. Nothing you choose is sent anywhere.

What this cannot do:
- It cannot tell you whether a real message or screen is genuine. Real apps look different, and they change.
- Scams change faster than any set of screens, so it teaches behaviours, not looks.
- In Europe, the name check covers euro transfers from banks in the euro area since 9 October 2025. Banks in other EU countries add it by 9 July 2027.
- In India, whether a fingerprint or your face can approve a payment depends on your bank and app. Any approval sends money.

If money has gone, the reporting route at the end is the one to use.
